entries.short: Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, was the ancestor of various Arab tribes. Though not the chosen heir, he was still blessed by God.
entries.article:
Ishmael was the first son of Abraham, born to him through Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian maidservant (<ref="Gen.16.15">Gen.16.15</ref>). His birth came after Sarah, who was barren, had given Hagar to Abraham to bear a child on her behalf. God spoke to Hagar, telling her to name the child Ishmael, meaning "God hears" (<ref="Gen.16.11">Gen.16.11</ref>). 

As he grew, Ishmael became a skilled archer (<ref="Gen.21.20">Gen.21.20</ref>). When Isaac was born to Sarah, she insisted that Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away (<ref="Gen.21.10">Gen.21.10</ref>). God confirmed this action but promised to make Ishmael a great nation (<ref="Gen.21.13,18">Gen.21.13,18</ref>). Ishmael settled in the wilderness of Paran and married an Egyptian woman (<ref="Gen.21.21">Gen.21.21</ref>). 

Ishmael had twelve sons who became tribal rulers (<ref="Gen.17.20">Gen.17.20</ref>; 25.13-16). He lived to be 137 years old (<ref="Gen.25.17">Gen.25.17</ref>). Ishmael and Isaac together buried their father Abraham (<ref="Gen.25.9">Gen.25.9</ref>). 

Ishmael's descendants, the Ishmaelites, are mentioned as traders who purchased Joseph from his brothers (<ref="Gen.37.25-28">Gen.37.25-28</ref>; 39.1). They are also noted as skilled archers (<ref="Isa.21.17">Isa.21.17</ref>) and as enemies of Israel (<ref="Psa.83.6">Psa.83.6</ref>). One of David's warriors, Zebadiah, was the son of an Ishmaelite (<ref="1Ch.2.17">1Ch.2.17</ref>; 27.30). 

Ishmael represents the ancestors of various Arab tribes. His story illustrates God's faithfulness to His promises, even to those not chosen for the primary covenant line.

entries.name: Israel
entries.brief: Patriarch, son of Isaac, father of twelve tribes
entries.short: Israel, also named Jacob, was the son of Isaac, the father of the twelve tribes of Israel, and a key patriarch of the Jewish people.
entries.article:
Israel, also known as Jacob, was the son of Isaac and Rebekah, and the grandson of Abraham. He was born after his twin brother Esau (Gen. 25:24-26). 

Jacob bought Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew when Esau was famished (Gen. 25:29-34). He then deceived his father Isaac into giving him the firstborn blessing (Gen. 27). To escape Esau's anger, Jacob fled to his uncle Laban in Paddan-aram (Gen. 28:1-5). 

On the way, Jacob had a dream of a stairway to heaven at Bethel, where God confirmed the covenant promises to him (Gen. 28:10-22). Jacob worked for Laban for 14 years, marrying his daughters Leah and Rachel (Gen. 29). 

Wanting to return home, Jacob left Paddan-aram with his family and flocks. On the way, he wrestled with God at Peniel and was renamed Israel, meaning "he struggles with God" (Gen. 32:22-32). Israel (or 'Jacob') reconciled with Esau and settled in Canaan (Gen. 33). 

Jacob had twelve sons who became the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad and Asher (Gen. 35:23-26). 

Jacob showed favoritism to Joseph, provoking his brothers to sell Joseph into slavery in Egypt (Gen. 37). Later, during a famine, Jacob's sons went to Egypt for food and were reconciled with Joseph, who had risen to power there (Gen. 42-46). 

Jacob moved his whole family to Egypt, where he lived for 17 years (Gen. 47:28). Before his death, Jacob blessed Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48) and gave prophetic blessings to his own twelve sons (Gen. 49). He died at age 147 and was buried in Canaan (Gen. 49:33; 50:1-14). 

God often identified Himself as the "God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" and reaffirmed His covenant promises to Jacob's descendants (e.g. Exo. 3:6,15). The nation of Israel took its name from Jacob and the Jewish people are his descendants. The name Jeshurun is used as a poetic name for Israel (Deut. 32:15; 33:5,26; Isa. 44:2).

entries.name: Ithran
entries.brief: Descendant of Esau, son of Dishon the Horite.
entries.short: Ithran was a descendant of Esau and son of Dishon the Horite.
entries.article:
Ithran is mentioned in two genealogical lists in the Bible as a descendant of Esau, the son of Isaac and twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob') (<ref="Gen.36.26">Gen.36.26</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.41">1Ch.1.41</ref>). He was the son of Dishon, who was a Horite, one of the inhabitants of the land of Seir before Esau's descendants settled there (<ref="Gen.36.20-21">Gen.36.20-21</ref>). 

The genealogies in Genesis 36 and 1Chronicles 1 record the descendants of Esau, also known as Edom, and the Horite tribes that intermarried with them. These lists demonstrate the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations (<ref="Gen.17.4-5">Gen.17.4-5</ref>). 

No other details are provided about Ithran's life or role within the clan. His inclusion in these genealogies serves to trace the lineage of Esau and the Edomites and to highlight the connection between the Israelites and their neighboring nations.

entries.name: Jalam
entries.brief: Son of Esau and Oholibamah
entries.short: Jalam was a son of Esau and Oholibamah, and a chief of Edom.
entries.article: Jalam was one of the sons born to Esau, the son of Isaac, and his wife Oholibamah, as recorded in <ref="Gen.36.5, 14">Gen.36.5, 14</ref>, and 18, and <ref="1Ch.1.35">1Ch.1.35</ref>. Esau, also known as Edom, settled in the region of Seir and became the ancestor of the Edomites. Jalam and his brothers, Jeush and Korah, were born in Canaan before Esau moved to Seir. <ref="Gen.36.18">Gen.36.18</ref> lists Jalam as one of the chiefs of Edom, indicating that he and his descendants held a position of authority within the Edomite tribal structure.

entries.name: Japheth
entries.brief: Son of Noah, ancestor of Indo-European peoples
entries.short: Japheth was one of Noah's three sons and the ancestor of the Indo-European peoples.
entries.article: Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah, along with Shem and Ham, as recorded in <ref="Gen.5.32">Gen.5.32</ref> and <ref="Gen.6.10">Gen.6.10</ref>. He and his brothers were born before the Great Flood. Japheth, his wife, and his brothers and their wives entered the ark with Noah and survived the Flood (<ref="Gen.7.13">Gen.7.13</ref>). After the Flood, Noah blessed Japheth, saying, "May God extend Japheth's territory; may Japheth live in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be the slave of Japheth" (<ref="Gen.9.27">Gen.9.27</ref>). Japheth's descendants are listed in <ref="Gen.10.2-5">Gen.10.2-5</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.5-7">1Ch.1.5-7</ref>, and they are generally associated with the Indo-European peoples, including the Greeks, Medes, and Thracians. The name Japheth means "enlargement" or "expansion," which is fitting given the widespread distribution of his descendants. Japheth's offspring played a significant role in the repopulation of the earth after the Flood and the development of various nations and cultures.

entries.name: Javan
entries.brief: Son of Japheth; ancestor of Greek people
entries.short: Javan, the ancestor of the Greek people, was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah.
entries.article: Javan is mentioned in the Table of Nations (<ref="Gen.10.2,4">Gen.10.2,4</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.5,7">1Ch.1.5,7</ref>) as one of the sons of Japheth and grandsons of Noah. He is considered the ancestor of the Greek people, and his name is often used in the Bible as a reference to Greece or the Greek people. In the Old Testament, Javan is associated with the trading of slaves (<ref="Jol.3.6">Jol.3.6</ref>), suggesting that the Greeks were involved in the slave trade. In the New Testament, the term "Greeks" (Hellenes) is used to refer to non-Jewish people, particularly those influenced by Greek culture. The Greeks are mentioned in various contexts, such as seeking Jesus (<ref="Jhn.12.20">Jhn.12.20</ref>), attending synagogues (<ref="Act.14.1; 17.4; 18.4">Act.14.1; 17.4; 18.4</ref>), and being among the first Gentile converts to Christianity (<ref="Act.16.1,3">Act.16.1,3</ref>). The inclusion of Greeks in the early church underscores the universal nature of the gospel message (<ref="Rom.1.16; 10.12">Rom.1.16; 10.12</ref>; <ref="Gal.3.28">Gal.3.28</ref>). The Greeks are also depicted as seekers of wisdom (<ref="1Co.1.22">1Co.1.22</ref>) and are contrasted with the Jews in terms of their religious and cultural background (<ref="Rom.1.14; 2.9-10">Rom.1.14; 2.9-10</ref>; <ref="1Co.10.32; 12.13">1Co.10.32; 12.13</ref>). In <ref="Mrk.7.26">Mrk.7.26</ref>, a Syrophoenician woman is described as a Greek, highlighting the widespread influence of Greek culture in the region.

entries.name: Jebusites
entries.brief: Canaanite tribe inhabiting Jerusalem before David's conquest
entries.short: The Jebusites were a Canaanite tribe that inhabited Jerusalem before King David conquered the city.
entries.article: The Jebusites were one of the Canaanite tribes that inhabited the land promised to the Israelites by God. They are first mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.16">Gen.10.16</ref> and <ref="Gen.15.21">Gen.15.21</ref> as descendants of Canaan, the grandson of Noah. When the Israelites left Egypt, God promised to drive out the Jebusites and other Canaanite tribes from the land (<ref="Exo.3.8, 17; 13.5; 23.23; 33.2; 34.11">Exo.3.8, 17; 13.5; 23.23; 33.2; 34.11</ref>). During the conquest of Canaan under Joshua, the Jebusites were among the tribes that the Israelites were commanded to utterly destroy (<ref="Deu.7.1; 20.17">Deu.7.1; 20.17</ref>). However, the Jebusites proved to be formidable opponents, and the Israelites were unable to completely drive them out of Jerusalem (<ref="Jos.15.63">Jos.15.63</ref>; <ref="Jdg.1.21">Jdg.1.21</ref>). The Jebusites continued to live among the Israelites during the time of the judges (<ref="Jdg.3.5; 19.11">Jdg.3.5; 19.11</ref>). It was not until the reign of King David that the Jebusites were finally defeated, and Jerusalem was captured and made the capital of Israel (<ref="2Sa.5.6-8">2Sa.5.6-8</ref>; <ref="1Ch.11.4-6">1Ch.11.4-6</ref>). After their defeat, some Jebusites remained in the land and were subjected to forced labor by Solomon (<ref="1Ki.9.20">1Ki.9.20</ref>; <ref="2Ch.8.7">2Ch.8.7</ref>). The site where the temple was built, Mount Moriah, was purchased by David from Araunah the Jebusite (<ref="2Sa.24.16-18">2Sa.24.16-18</ref>; <ref="1Ch.21.15-28">1Ch.21.15-28</ref>; <ref="2Ch.3.1">2Ch.3.1</ref>). The Jebusites are mentioned among the foreign peoples with whom the Israelites intermarried, contrary to God's command (<ref="Ezr.9.1">Ezr.9.1</ref>). In <ref="Zec.9.7">Zec.9.7</ref>, there is a prophetic promise that the Jebusites will be incorporated into God's people, symbolizing the inclusion of Gentiles in the future messianic kingdom.

entries.name: Jerah
entries.brief: A son of Joktan, descendant of Shem.
entries.short: Jerah was one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem, as recorded in the Table of Nations in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jerah is mentioned in the Table of Nations in Genesis and 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem, the son of Noah. Joktan's descendants are believed to have settled in the southern Arabian Peninsula, suggesting that Jerah and his brothers may have been associated with the ancient peoples of that region. However, no further details are provided about Jerah's life or the specific territory he and his descendants inhabited.

entries.name: Jetheth
entries.brief: A chief of Edom
entries.short: Jetheth, one of the chiefs of Edom.
entries.article: Jetheth is mentioned in the lists of the chiefs of Edom in <ref="Gen.36.40">Gen.36.40</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.51">1Ch.1.51</ref>. He is identified as one of the chiefs who came from the Edomite clans.

entries.name: Jetur
entries.brief: Son of Ishmael
entries.short: Jetur, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael.
entries.article: Jetur is mentioned in the genealogies of Ishmael in <ref="Gen.25.15">Gen.25.15</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.31">1Ch.1.31</ref>. He is listed as one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. The Ishmaelites, including Jetur and his brothers, are described as living in the region from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt (<ref="Gen.25.18">Gen.25.18</ref>).

entries.name: Jeush
entries.brief: Son of Esau and Oholibamah
entries.short: Jeush, a son of Esau and Oholibamah, was a chief of Edom.
entries.article: Jeush was one of the sons of Esau, the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob'), and Esau's wife Oholibamah, as recorded in <ref="Gen.36.5,14">Gen.36.5,14</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.35">1Ch.1.35</ref>. He is listed among the chiefs of Edom who descended from Esau. As a grandson of Isaac and great-grandson of Abraham, Jeush was part of the Edomite clan that settled in the region of Seir.

entries.name: Jobab
entries.brief: A son of Joktan, descendant of Shem
entries.short: Jobab, a descendant of Shem through Joktan, is mentioned in the Table of Nations.
entries.article: Jobab is mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.29">Gen.10.29</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.23">1Ch.1.23</ref> as one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem. He is listed among the thirteen sons of Joktan in the genealogical record known as the Table of Nations. This record provides insight into the peoples and nations that descended from Noah's sons after the Flood. The descendants of Joktan are believed to have settled in the southern regions of the Arabian Peninsula.

entries.name: Jokshan
entries.brief: A son of Abraham and Keturah
entries.short: Jokshan was one of the sons born to Abraham and his wife Keturah after the death of Sarah.
entries.article:
Jokshan is mentioned in the Old Testament as one of the sons of Abraham and his wife Keturah. After the death of Sarah, Abraham took Keturah as his wife, and she bore him several children, including Jokshan (<ref="Gen.25.1-2">Gen.25.1-2</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.32">1Ch.1.32</ref>). 

The biblical record provides little information about Jokshan beyond his lineage. In <ref="Gen.25.3">Gen.25.3</ref>, it is stated that Jokshan became the father of Sheba and Dedan, suggesting that he had descendants who formed tribes or clans. The names Sheba and Dedan are associated with regions in Arabia, indicating that Jokshan's descendants may have settled in that area. 

Jokshan's mention in the genealogies of Abraham serves to highlight the fulfillment of God's promise to make Abraham the father of many nations (<ref="Gen.17.4-6">Gen.17.4-6</ref>). Although the covenant line would pass through Isaac and Israel (or 'Jacob'), Abraham's other sons, including Jokshan, are not forgotten in the biblical narrative. 

The fact that Jokshan and his brothers are listed in both Genesis and 1 Chronicles underscores the importance of genealogical records in ancient Israelite society. These records served to establish family ties, document the fulfillment of divine promises, and trace the origins of various tribes and nations. 

Beyond these details, the Bible does not provide any further information about Jokshan's life, his relationship with his father Abraham, or the specific history of his descendants. His inclusion in the biblical record serves primarily to paint a more complete picture of Abraham's family and the nations that descended from him.

entries.name: Joktan
entries.brief: Son of Eber and ancestor of Arabian tribes
entries.short: Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, was the ancestor of several Arabian tribes.
entries.article:
Joktan is mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis 10 and 1Chronicles 1 as a descendant of Shem, the son of Noah. He was the son of Eber and the brother of Peleg (<ref="Gen.10.25">Gen.10.25</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.19">1Ch.1.19</ref>). The biblical record states that in the days of Peleg, the earth was divided, possibly referring to the division of languages and nations at the Tower of Babel (<ref="Gen.10.25">Gen.10.25</ref>). 

Joktan is described as the ancestor of several Arabian tribes. <ref="Gen.10.26-29">Gen.10.26-29</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.20-23">1Ch.1.20-23</ref> list his 13 sons: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. These names are associated with various regions in Arabia, suggesting that Joktan's descendants settled in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. 

The mention of Joktan and his sons in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10) serves to highlight the diversity of peoples and nations that descended from Noah's sons after the Flood. It also demonstrates the fulfillment of God's command to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (<ref="Gen.9.1">Gen.9.1</ref>). 

Although no further details are provided about Joktan's life or his relationship with his descendants, his inclusion in the biblical genealogies emphasizes the connection between the Semitic peoples and the Arabian tribes. It also underscores the importance of genealogical records in ancient Near Eastern societies for establishing family ties and tracing the origins of nations.

entries.name: Kedar
entries.brief: A son of Ishmael and a nomadic tribe
entries.short: Kedar was a son of Ishmael and the eponymous ancestor of a nomadic Arab tribe known for their tents and flocks.
entries.article:
Kedar is first mentioned in <ref="Gen.25.13">Gen.25.13</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.29">1Ch.1.29</ref> as one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham. He is the eponymous ancestor of the Kedarites, a nomadic Arab tribe that inhabited the desert regions of northern Arabia. 

The Kedarites were known for their black tents (<ref="Sng.1.5">Sng.1.5</ref>) and their large flocks of sheep and goats (<ref="Isa.60.7">Isa.60.7</ref>; <ref="Ezk.27.21">Ezk.27.21</ref>). They were skilled archers and warriors (<ref="Isa.21.16-17">Isa.21.16-17</ref>) and were one of the major Arab tribes in the ancient Near East. 

In the Bible, Kedar is often used as a representation of the nomadic tribes of the desert. The psalmist laments living among the tents of Kedar, symbolizing a hostile and foreign environment (Psalm <ref="Isa.120.5">Isa.120.5</ref>). The prophet Jeremiah uses Kedar as an example of a distant and powerful nation.

entries.name: Kedemah
entries.brief: A son of Ishmael; Nodab, a Hagrite tribe
entries.short: Kedemah was a son of Ishmael, while the Nodab were a Hagrite tribe defeated by the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh.
entries.article:
Kedemah is mentioned in <ref="Gen.25.15">Gen.25.15</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.31">1Ch.1.31</ref> as one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham. He is listed along with his brothers as the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Ishmael. 

Apart from these genealogical mentions, no further information is provided about Kedemah's life or the specific tribe that descended from him. 

Nodab, on the other hand, is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.5.19">1Ch.5.19</ref> as one of the Hagrite tribes that the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought against during the days of Saul. The Israelite tribes defeated the Hagrites and took captive their livestock and tents. 

The Hagrites were a nomadic people who lived in the region east of Gilead. The mention of Nodab alongside the Hagrites suggests that they were likely a subgroup or an allied tribe of the Hagrites. 

Apart from this brief mention in the context of the Israelite tribes' victory over the Hagrites, no other information is provided about the Nodab tribe in the Bible.

entries.name: Kenan
entries.brief: Son of Enosh, descendant of Seth
entries.short: Kenan (Cainan), the son of Enosh, was a descendant of Seth and an ancestor of Noah.
entries.article: Kenan, also known as Cainan, was a descendant of Seth, the third son of Adam and Eve (Gen. 5:9, 10, 12, 13, 14; 1Chr. 1:2; <ref="Luk.3.37">Luk.3.37</ref>). He was the son of Enosh and the father of Mahalalel. The genealogy in Genesis 5 provides the ages at which Kenan and other pre-flood patriarchs had children and the total length of their lives. Kenan was 70 years old when he became the father of Mahalalel, and he lived a total of 910 years (Gen. <ref="Luk.5.12-14">Luk.5.12-14</ref>). The long lifespans of the pre-flood patriarchs are a distinctive feature of this genealogy and may indicate a different environment or a closer genetic connection to the original creation. Kenan's inclusion in the genealogies of both Genesis and 1 Chronicles highlights the importance of tracing the lineage from Adam to Noah, and ultimately to Abraham, the father of the Israelites. His name also appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ in <ref="Luk.3.37">Luk.3.37</ref>, emphasizing the connection between Jesus and the ancestral line of humanity.

entries.name: Kenaz
entries.brief: An Edomite clan descended from Esau
entries.short: Kenaz was one of the clans of Edom, descended from Esau through his son Eliphaz.
entries.article:
Kenaz is mentioned in Genesis 36 and 1Chronicles 1 as one of the clans of Edom, descended from Esau. In the genealogy of Esau, Kenaz is listed as one of the sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau (<ref="Gen.36.11, 15">Gen.36.11, 15</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.36">1Ch.1.36</ref>). 

The Kenizzites, the clan named after Kenaz, are also mentioned among the chiefs of Edom (<ref="Gen.36.42">Gen.36.42</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.53">1Ch.1.53</ref>), indicating their prominence and leadership within the Edomite tribal structure. 

The inclusion of Kenaz and the Kenizzites in the genealogy of Esau highlights the development and growth of the Edomite people, who were the descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother. 

Apart from these genealogical mentions, no further information is provided about the specific history, territory, or activities of the Kenizzite clan in the Bible.

entries.name: Keturah
entries.brief: Abraham's concubine after Sarah's death
entries.short: Keturah was the concubine Abraham took after the death of Sarah, and she bore him six sons.
entries.article:
Keturah is mentioned in <ref="Gen.25.1, 4">Gen.25.1, 4</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.32, 33">1Ch.1.32, 33</ref> as the concubine Abraham took after the death of Sarah. She is described as Abraham's concubine, which in the context of the ancient Near East, was a secondary wife with legal rights and status. 

Keturah bore Abraham six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (<ref="Gen.25.2">Gen.25.2</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.32">1Ch.1.32</ref>). These sons became the ancestors of various tribes and nations, expanding Abraham's descendants beyond the primary line of Isaac and Ishmael. 

Abraham gave gifts to the sons of Keturah and sent them away to the east, separating them from his son Isaac to avoid conflict over the inheritance (<ref="Gen.25.6">Gen.25.6</ref>). This action ensured that Isaac, the child of promise, would be the primary heir of Abraham's legacy and covenant blessings. 

The mention of Keturah and her sons in the genealogies of Abraham demonstrates the fulfillment of God's promise to make Abraham a father of many nations (<ref="Gen.17.4-6">Gen.17.4-6</ref>). It also highlights the complexity of family relationships and the importance of preserving the line of Isaac as the chosen heir of the covenant promises.

entries.name: Kittim
entries.brief: Descendants of Javan, son of Japheth
entries.short: Kittim, a descendant of Japheth, son of Noah.
entries.article: Kittim was a son of Javan and grandson of Japheth, son of Noah (<ref="Gen.10.4">Gen.10.4</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.7">1Ch.1.7</ref>). The Kittim are listed among the descendants of Japheth who spread out into their lands after the flood, each with their own language, clan, and nation (<ref="Gen.10.5">Gen.10.5</ref>). The Kittim likely settled in the area of Cyprus, as Kittim is an early name for this island. They were probably a seafaring People from Japheth.

entries.name: Korah
entries.brief: Son of Esau
entries.short: Korah, son of Esau and Oholibamah
entries.article: Korah was a son of Esau and his wife Oholibamah (<ref="Gen.36.5, 18">Gen.36.5, 18</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.35">1Ch.1.35</ref>). He was born in Canaan before Esau moved his family to Seir (<ref="Gen.36.5-8">Gen.36.5-8</ref>). Korah was a grandson of Zibeon the Hivite (<ref="Gen.36.14">Gen.36.14</ref>). He became one of the chiefs of Edom (<ref="Gen.36.18">Gen.36.18</ref>).

entries.name: Lamech
entries.brief: Father of Noah; lived 777 years
entries.short: Lamech, the father of Noah, lived 777 years.
entries.article: Lamech was the son of Methuselah and the father of Noah (<ref="Gen.5.25,28-29">Gen.5.25,28-29</ref>). He was born when Methuselah was 187 years old (<ref="Gen.5.25">Gen.5.25</ref>). Lamech named his son Noah, saying, "This one will comfort us in the labor and painful toil of our hands caused by the ground the Lord has cursed" (<ref="Gen.5.29">Gen.5.29</ref>). Lamech lived 595 years after the birth of Noah and had other sons and daughters (<ref="Gen.5.30">Gen.5.30</ref>). He died at the age of 777, making him the second-oldest person mentioned in the Bible after his father, Methuselah (<ref="Gen.5.31">Gen.5.31</ref>). Lamech is also mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus Christ in the Gospel of Luke (<ref="Luk.3.36">Luk.3.36</ref>) and in the genealogy of Adam in the book of Chronicles (<ref="1Ch.1.3">1Ch.1.3</ref>). His life and legacy are significant in the context of the pre-flood world and the lineage of the patriarchs leading to Noah.

entries.name: Lehabim
entries.brief: Son of Mizraim; progenitor of a people group
entries.short: Lehabim, a son of Mizraim and progenitor of a people group.
entries.article: Lehabim was one of the sons of Mizraim, who was a son of Ham (<ref="Gen.10.13">Gen.10.13</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.11">1Ch.1.11</ref>). He is mentioned in the Table of Nations, which records the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Lehabim is listed among the descendants of Ham, specifically as a son of Mizraim, who is associated with Egypt. The Lehabim are believed to be the ancestors of the Libyans, a people group that inhabited the region west of Egypt in North Africa. However, the exact relationship between the Lehabim and the historical Libyans is not certain.

entries.name: Lotan
entries.brief: Son of Seir the Horite; chief of Edom
entries.short: Lotan, a son of Seir the Horite and a chief of Edom.
entries.article: Lotan was a son of Seir the Horite and a chief of the land of Edom (<ref="Gen.36.20,29">Gen.36.20,29</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.38">1Ch.1.38</ref>). He had a sister named Timna (<ref="Gen.36.22">Gen.36.22</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.39">1Ch.1.39</ref>). Lotan is listed among the descendants of Esau who settled in the region of Seir (<ref="Gen.36.20-30">Gen.36.20-30</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.38-42">1Ch.1.38-42</ref>). The Horites were the original inhabitants of Seir before Esau's descendants displaced them (Deut <ref="2.12">2.12</ref>). As a chief of Edom, Lotan likely held a position of authority and influence among his people.

entries.name: Lud
entries.brief: Son of Shem; progenitor of the Lydians
entries.short: Lud, a son of Shem and progenitor of the Lydians.
entries.article: Lud was one of the sons of Shem, the son of Noah (<ref="Gen.10.22">Gen.10.22</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.17">1Ch.1.17</ref>). He is mentioned in the Table of Nations, which records the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Lud is considered the ancestor of the Lydians, a people group that inhabited the region of Lydia in western Anatolia (modern-day Turkey). The Lydians were known for their military prowess and are mentioned as allies or mercenaries of Tyre and Egypt (<ref="Ezk.27.10">Ezk.27.10</ref>; 30.5; <ref="Jer.46.9">Jer.46.9</ref>). The prophet Isaiah also includes Lud among the nations that will come to know the glory of the Lord (<ref="Isa.66.19">Isa.66.19</ref>). Although the connection between the biblical Lud and the historical Lydians is not explicitly stated, it is generally accepted based on the similarity of the names and the geographic location associated with Lud's descendants.

entries.name: Ludim
entries.brief: Son of Mizraim; progenitor of a people group
entries.short: Ludim, a son of Mizraim and progenitor of a people group.
entries.article: Ludim was one of the sons of Mizraim, who was a son of Ham (<ref="Gen.10.13">Gen.10.13</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.11">1Ch.1.11</ref>). He is mentioned in the Table of Nations, which records the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Ludim is listed among the descendants of Ham, specifically as a son of Mizraim, who is associated with Egypt. The Ludim are believed to be the ancestors of the Lydians, a people group that inhabited the region of Lydia in western Anatolia (modern-day Turkey). However, the exact relationship between the Ludim and the historical Lydians is not certain.

entries.name: Madai
entries.brief: Son of Japheth; progenitor of the Medes
entries.short: Madai, a son of Japheth, is considered the ancestor of the Medes.
entries.article: Madai is mentioned in the Table of Nations (Gen.10) and the genealogy of Chronicles (1Ch.1) as one of the sons of Japheth, the son of Noah. He is considered the ancestor of the Medes, an ancient Iranian people who inhabited the region of Media in western Iran. The Medes played a significant role in the ancient Near East, forming a powerful empire and later contributing to the Persian Empire. In the Bible, the Medes are known for their role in the fall of Babylon, as prophesied by Isaiah and Jeremiah (<ref="Isa.13.17">Isa.13.17</ref>; <ref="Jer.51.11,28">Jer.51.11,28</ref>). The inclusion of Madai in the Table of Nations and the genealogy of Chronicles emphasizes the biblical understanding of the origins and relationships of the various nations and people groups in the ancient world. As a descendant of Japheth, Madai is part of the lineage that spread out and populated the coastlands and islands, as described in Genesis 10.5.

entries.name: Magdiel
entries.brief: Edomite chief descended from Esau
entries.short: Magdiel was an Edomite chief, a descendant of Esau, the son of Isaac.
entries.article: Magdiel is mentioned in the lists of Edomite chiefs found in Genesis 36 and 1Chronicles 1. He is identified as one of the chiefs of Edom, a descendant of Esau, the son of Isaac and the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob') (<ref="Gen.36.43">Gen.36.43</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.54">1Ch.1.54</ref>). The Edomites were the descendants of Esau who settled in the region of Seir, south of the Dead Sea. The lists of Edomite chiefs provide a record of the political and social structure of Edom, highlighting the importance of family lineage and tribal leadership. Magdiel's inclusion in these lists suggests that he held a position of authority and influence within the Edomite community. However, no further details are provided about his personal life, achievements, or the specific period of his leadership. The mention of Magdiel in these genealogical records serves to establish the continuity of Esau's descendants and their role in the history of the region.

entries.name: Magog
entries.brief: Son of Japheth; progenitor of a people group
entries.short: Magog, a son of Japheth, is considered the ancestor of a people group mentioned in Ezekiel's prophecy.
entries.article: Magog is mentioned in the Table of Nations (Gen.10) and the genealogy of Chronicles (1Ch.1) as one of the sons of Japheth, the son of Noah. He is considered the ancestor of a people group that bore his name. In the Bible, the name Magog appears in the prophetic context of Ezekiel 38-39, where Magog is described as a land ruled by Gog, a powerful leader who will lead a coalition of nations against Israel in the end times. The exact identity of the Magog people and their geographical location is uncertain, but some scholars suggest that they may have been associated with the Scythians, a nomadic people who inhabited the region north of the Black Sea. The inclusion of Magog in the Table of Nations and the genealogy of Chronicles emphasizes the biblical understanding of the origins and relationships of the various nations and people groups in the ancient world. As a descendant of Japheth, Magog is part of the lineage that spread out and populated the coastlands and islands, as described in Genesis 10.5.

entries.name: Mahalalel
entries.brief: Descendant of Seth; ancestor of Noah
entries.short: Mahalalel was a descendant of Seth and an ancestor of Noah, living before the flood.
entries.article: Mahalalel is mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis 5, 1Chronicles 1, and Luke 3 as a descendant of Seth, the third son of Adam and Eve. He is an ancestor of Noah and is part of the lineage that leads to Abraham, David, and ultimately, Jesus Christ. According to Genesis 5, Mahalalel was the son of Kenan and the father of Jared (<ref="Gen.5.12,15">Gen.5.12,15</ref>). He lived for 895 years, which was typical of the long lifespans recorded for the pre-flood patriarchs (<ref="Gen.5.13,16,17">Gen.5.13,16,17</ref>). The genealogies in Genesis 5 and 1Chronicles 1 focus on the line of descent from Adam to Noah, highlighting the continuity of the godly lineage before the flood. The genealogy in Luke 3 traces Jesus' ancestry back to Adam, emphasizing His connection to all of humanity. Mahalalel's inclusion in these genealogies serves to establish the historical and theological context of God's plan of redemption through the descendants of Seth, ultimately leading to the birth of Jesus Christ.

entries.name: Manahath
entries.brief: Son of Shobal, a Horite.
entries.short: Manahath was a son of Shobal, a Horite.
entries.article: Manahath was a Horite, a descendant of Seir, who lived in the land of Edom. He was the son of Shobal and is mentioned in the genealogies of the Horites (<ref="Gen.36.23">Gen.36.23</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.40">1Ch.1.40</ref>).

entries.name: Massa
entries.brief: Son of Ishmael, grandson of Abraham.
entries.short: Massa, a son of Ishmael, was a grandson of Abraham.
entries.article: Massa was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar. He is mentioned in the genealogies of Ishmael's descendants (<ref="Gen.25.14">Gen.25.14</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.30">1Ch.1.30</ref>). As a grandson of Abraham, Massa was part of the Ishmaelite tribes that settled in the Arabian Peninsula.

entries.name: Matred
entries.brief: Mother of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar, king of Edom.
entries.short: Matred was the mother of Mehetabel, who was the wife of Hadar, king of Edom.
entries.article: Matred was a woman mentioned in the genealogies of the kings of Edom. She was the mother of Mehetabel, who became the wife of Hadar (or Hadad), the last king of Edom mentioned before the monarchy of Israel (<ref="Gen.36.39">Gen.36.39</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.50">1Ch.1.50</ref>).

entries.name: Medan
entries.brief: Son of Abraham and Keturah.
entries.short: Medan was a son of Abraham and his concubine Keturah.
entries.article: Medan was one of the sons born to Abraham and his concubine Keturah after the death of Sarah. Along with his brothers Zimran, Jokshan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah, Medan was sent away by Abraham with gifts to the land of the east, separating them from Isaac, Abraham's son with Sarah (<ref="Gen.25.1-6">Gen.25.1-6</ref>). Medan is also mentioned in the genealogy of Abraham's descendants in <ref="1Ch.1.32">1Ch.1.32</ref>. Little else is known about Medan or his descendants, as they are not mentioned further in the biblical narrative.

entries.name: Mehetabel
entries.brief: Wife of Hadar, king of Edom.
entries.short: Mehetabel was the wife of Hadar, a king of Edom.
entries.article: Mehetabel was the wife of Hadar (or Hadad), who was the last king of Edom mentioned in the genealogy of Esau. She was the daughter of Matred and the granddaughter of Me-zahab (<ref="Gen.36.39">Gen.36.39</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.50">1Ch.1.50</ref>). The Edomites were descendants of Esau, the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob'), and they settled in the region southeast of Judah. The mention of Mehetabel in the genealogy suggests that she held a significant position as the queen of Edom during her husband's reign. However, no further details about her life or role are provided in the biblical text.

entries.name: Meshech
entries.brief: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah.
entries.short: Meshech, a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, is mentioned in the Table of Nations.
entries.article: Meshech was one of the sons of Japheth and a grandson of Noah, mentioned in the Table of Nations (<ref="Gen.10.2">Gen.10.2</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.5">1Ch.1.5</ref>). The Table of Nations is a genealogical record of the descendants of Noah's three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and their dispersal after the Tower of Babel. Meshech is listed among the sons of Japheth, along with his brothers Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, and Tiras. These sons and their descendants are generally associated with the peoples of the northern and western regions, including Asia Minor and Europe.

entries.name: Methuselah
entries.brief: The oldest person mentioned in the Bible.
entries.short: Methuselah, the son of Enoch, was the oldest person mentioned in the Bible, living 969 years.
entries.article: Methuselah, the son of Enoch and the grandfather of Noah, is recognized as the oldest person mentioned in the Bible. He lived an astonishing 969 years (<ref="Gen.5.27">Gen.5.27</ref>). Methuselah's father, Enoch, walked with God and was taken by Him at the age of 365 (<ref="Gen.5.21-24">Gen.5.21-24</ref>). Methuselah's long life is seen as a symbol of God's patience and mercy in delaying the judgment of the flood until after his death. His name is mentioned in the genealogies of both Chronicles (<ref="1Ch.1.3">1Ch.1.3</ref>) and Luke (<ref="Luk.3.37">Luk.3.37</ref>), emphasizing his importance in the lineage of the Messiah. Although little is known about Methuselah's personal life or character, his exceptional longevity stands as a testament to God's sovereignty and the reliability of His word.

entries.name: Mezahab
entries.brief: Grandfather of Mehetabel, wife of Edomite king Hadar.
entries.short: Mezahab was the grandfather of Mehetabel, who was the wife of Hadar, an Edomite king.
entries.article: Mezahab is mentioned in the genealogies of Esau in the book of Genesis and the book of Chronicles (<ref="Gen.36.39">Gen.36.39</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.50">1Ch.1.50</ref>). He was the father of Matred and the grandfather of Mehetabel, who became the wife of Hadar, the last king of Edom mentioned in these genealogies. No further information is given about Mezahab's life, occupation, or place of origin. His name, which means "waters of gold" or "gold waters" in Hebrew, may suggest some connection to a place known for its gold or water resources, but the Bible does not provide any details to confirm this.

entries.name: Mibsam
entries.brief: Son of Ishmael, grandson of Abraham.
entries.short: Mibsam was a son of Ishmael and grandson of Abraham.
entries.article: Mibsam is mentioned in the genealogies of Ishmael, the son of Abraham, in the books of Genesis and 1 Chronicles (<ref="Gen.25.13">Gen.25.13</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.29">1Ch.1.29</ref>). He was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, who were described as "princes according to their nations" (<ref="Gen.25.16">Gen.25.16</ref>). The listing of Ishmael's sons demonstrates the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham that He would make Ishmael fruitful and multiply him exceedingly (<ref="Gen.17.20">Gen.17.20</ref>).

entries.name: Mibzar
entries.brief: A chief of Edom, descendant of Esau.
entries.short: Mibzar was one of the chiefs of Edom, descended from Esau.
entries.article: Mibzar is mentioned in the lists of the chiefs of Edom in the books of Genesis and 1 Chronicles (<ref="Gen.36.42">Gen.36.42</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.53">1Ch.1.53</ref>). He was one of the chiefs who came from the descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother. The Edomites were the offspring of Esau and lived in the region southeast of Israel. The chiefs of Edom are listed to show the political and social structure of the Edomite people. No specific details are provided about Mibzar's life, reign, or achievements. His inclusion in the list of chiefs suggests he held a position of authority and leadership among the Edomites.

entries.name: Midian
entries.brief: Son of Abraham and Keturah; father of the Midianites.
entries.short: Midian, a son of Abraham and Keturah, was the ancestor of the Midianite people.
entries.article: Midian was a son of Abraham and his second wife, Keturah (<ref="Gen.25.2">Gen.25.2</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.32">1Ch.1.32</ref>). He was born after the death of Sarah and is listed among Abraham's sons by Keturah, along with Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Ishbak, and Shuah. Midian had five sons: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah (<ref="Gen.25.4">Gen.25.4</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.33">1Ch.1.33</ref>). These sons became the ancestors of the Midianite tribes, who are mentioned throughout the Old Testament. The Midianites lived in the desert regions of the Arabian Peninsula and were known for their nomadic lifestyle and involvement in trade. They played a significant role in the stories of Joseph (<ref="Gen.37.28,36">Gen.37.28,36</ref>) and Moses (<ref="Exo.2.15-3">Exo.2.15-3</ref>.1). Later, the Midianites oppressed Israel during the time of the judges, until Gideon defeated them (Jdg.6-8). The descendants of Midian, the Midianites, were a prominent people group in the ancient Near East, and their interactions with the Israelites shaped various events in biblical history.

entries.name: Mishma
entries.brief: A son of Ishmael, Abraham's son.
entries.short: Mishma was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, and is listed among the chiefs of the Ishmaelite tribes.
entries.article:
Mishma was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, who was the son of Abraham by his concubine Hagar (<ref="Gen.25.14">Gen.25.14</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.30">1Ch.1.30</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogies of Ishmael, which record the names of Ishmael's sons and their descendants, who became the chiefs of the Ishmaelite tribes. 

The listing of Mishma and his brothers in these genealogies highlights the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham that Ishmael would be the father of twelve rulers and that his descendants would become a great nation (<ref="Gen.17.20">Gen.17.20</ref>). These twelve tribes, each headed by one of Ishmael's sons, likely inhabited the Arabian Peninsula and played a significant role in the region's history and culture. 

Apart from being named as a son of Ishmael and a tribal chief, no further details are provided about Mishma's life, character, or specific role within the Ishmaelite community. Nonetheless, his inclusion in the biblical record affirms his place in the family line of Abraham and the unfolding of God's plan for Ishmael's descendants.

entries.name: Mizzah
entries.brief: A grandson of Esau and a chief of Edom.
entries.short: Mizzah was a grandson of Esau and one of the chiefs of Edom listed in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.article:
Mizzah is mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.13,17">Gen.36.13,17</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.37">1Ch.1.37</ref> as one of the grandsons of Esau and a chief of Edom. He was the son of Reuel, who was one of Esau's sons by his wife Basemath. 

The genealogies in these passages list the descendants of Esau, who was also known as Edom, and provide insight into the family structure and leadership of the Edomite people. Mizzah is named among the chiefs of Edom, indicating that he held a position of authority and influence within the tribe. 

As a grandson of Esau, Mizzah was part of the second generation of Edomites and likely played a role in the establishment and growth of the Edomite kingdom. The Edomites were closely related to the Israelites, as Esau was the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob') (Israel), but they often had a contentious relationship throughout their history. 

Apart from being listed in these genealogies, no further details are provided about Mizzah's life, achievements, or specific role as a chief of Edom. However, his inclusion in these records highlights the importance of family lineage and tribal leadership in the ancient Near East.

entries.name: Nahath
entries.brief: A descendant of Esau, a chief of Edom.
entries.short: Nahath, a descendant of Esau, was one of the chiefs of Edom.
entries.article:
Nahath is mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.13,17">Gen.36.13,17</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.37">1Ch.1.37</ref> as one of the descendants of Esau and a chief of Edom. He was the son of Reuel, who was one of Esau's sons by his wife Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael. 

The genealogical records in these passages provide insight into the family lines of Esau, who was the brother of Israel (or 'Jacob') and the ancestor of the Edomites. Esau settled in the region of Seir, south of the Dead Sea, and his descendants became the rulers and chiefs of Edom. 

As a chief of Edom, Nahath would have held a position of authority and leadership within the Edomite tribal structure. The chiefs of Edom were likely responsible for governing their respective clans, making decisions on behalf of their people, and representing their interests in dealings with other tribes or nations. 

Apart from being listed in these genealogies, no additional information is provided about Nahath's life, character, or specific actions. His inclusion in the record serves to highlight the development and growth of Esau's descendants into a significant nation, as well as to provide a historical context for the relationship between the Israelites and the Edomites.

entries.name: Nahor
entries.brief: Son of Serug; father of Terah, Abraham's father.
entries.short: Nahor, the son of Serug and father of Terah, was Abraham's grandfather.
entries.article:
Nahor, mentioned in <ref="Gen.11.22-25">Gen.11.22-25</ref>, <ref="Jos.24.2, 1">Jos.24.2, 1</ref> Chronicles <ref="Jos.1.26">Jos.1.26</ref>, and <ref="Luk.3.34">Luk.3.34</ref>, was the son of Serug and the father of Terah. He was the grandfather of Abraham, the patriarch of the Israelites. 

According to the genealogical records in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, Nahor was born to Serug when Serug was 30 years old. Nahor himself became the father of Terah at the age of 29 and lived for a total of 148 years. 

In <ref="Jos.24.2">Jos.24.2</ref>, it is mentioned that Terah and his family, including Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates River and served other gods. This suggests that Nahor and his family were originally polytheistic and not worshippers of the one true God. 

Nahor's significance in the biblical narrative lies primarily in his role as a direct ancestor of Abraham. His inclusion in the genealogies of Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Luke demonstrates the importance of tracing the lineage of the patriarchs and establishing the continuity of God's plan through the generations.

entries.name: Naphish
entries.brief: Son of Ishmael, defeated by Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites.
entries.short: Naphish, a son of Ishmael, was among the Hagrite tribes defeated by the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
entries.article:
Naphish was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar (<ref="Gen.25.15">Gen.25.15</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.31">1Ch.1.31</ref>). As a descendant of Ishmael, Naphish would have been a member of the Ishmaelite tribes that settled in the Arabian Peninsula. 

In <ref="1Ch.5.19">1Ch.5.19</ref>, Naphish is mentioned in the context of a war between the Israelite tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. These tribes were likely Ishmaelite clans living east of the Jordan River. 

The Israelite tribes, trusting in God's help, went to war against these Hagrite tribes and were victorious. They captured a large number of livestock and took many people captive. The victory was attributed to God's intervention, as the Israelites had cried out to Him during the battle (<ref="1Ch.5.20">1Ch.5.20</ref>). 

Apart from these brief mentions, little else is known about Naphish or his specific role in the events described. His inclusion in the biblical record serves to highlight the ongoing interactions and conflicts between the Israelites and the surrounding tribes, as well as to demonstrate God's faithfulness to His people when they sought His help.

entries.name: Naphtuhim
entries.brief: Descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham
entries.short: The Naphtuhim were descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham, who settled in northern Egypt.
entries.article: The Naphtuhim are mentioned in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10) as one of the peoples descending from Mizraim, son of Ham (<ref="Gen.10.13, 1">Gen.10.13, 1</ref> Chronicles <ref="Gen.1.11">Gen.1.11</ref>). Mizraim was the ancestor of the Egyptians, so the Naphtuhim were one of the people groups that inhabited Egypt. Their exact location is uncertain, but some scholars place them in the Nile delta region of northern Egypt. No other details are given about their history or culture in the Bible. The Naphtuhim likely assimilated into Egyptian civilization over time.

entries.name: Nebaioth
entries.brief: Firstborn son of Ishmael; father of a tribe.
entries.short: Nebaioth, the firstborn son of Ishmael, was the ancestor of a tribe known for their flocks and mentioned in Isaiah's prophecy of future blessing.
entries.article:
Nebaioth was the firstborn son of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar (<ref="Gen.25.13">Gen.25.13</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.29">1Ch.1.29</ref>). As a descendant of Abraham through Ishmael, Nebaioth became the ancestor of a nomadic tribe that bore his name. 

The Nebaioth tribe was known for their large flocks of sheep and goats, which were highly prized for their wool and hair. In <ref="Isa.60.7">Isa.60.7</ref>, the prophet foretells a time of future blessing and restoration for Israel, mentioning that the flocks of Nebaioth will be gathered to Jerusalem and offered on the altar, finding acceptance with God. 

Nebaioth is also mentioned in connection with Esau, the son of Isaac and the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob'). According to <ref="Gen.28.9">Gen.28.9</ref> and <ref="Gen.36.3">Gen.36.3</ref>, Esau married Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael and the sister of Nebaioth, in addition to his other wives. This marriage alliance may have strengthened the ties between the Edomites (descendants of Esau) and the Ishmaelite tribes. 

As a nomadic tribe, the descendants of Nebaioth likely inhabited the regions of northern Arabia and the Negev desert. They were part of the larger group of Ishmaelite tribes that played a significant role in the trade and commerce of the ancient Near East. 

While little is known about Nebaioth as an individual, his legacy as the ancestor of a prominent tribe reflects the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham that his descendants through Ishmael would also become great nations (<ref="Gen.17.20">Gen.17.20</ref>). The inclusion of the Nebaioth tribe in Isaiah's prophecy suggests that they will have a place in God's future plans for Israel and the nations.

entries.name: Nimrod
entries.brief: Mighty hunter, built cities
entries.short: Nimrod was a mighty hunter and ruler who built several notable cities, including Babel and Nineveh.
entries.article: Nimrod was a descendant of Cush, the son of Ham (<ref="Gen.10.8">Gen.10.8</ref>). He was described as a mighty hunter before the Lord, indicating his prowess and skill (<ref="Gen.10.9">Gen.10.9</ref>). Nimrod became a powerful ruler, establishing a kingdom that included the cities of Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (<ref="Gen.10.10">Gen.10.10</ref>). He also expanded his kingdom to Assyria, where he built the cities of Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah, and Resen (<ref="Gen.10.11-12">Gen.10.11-12</ref>). The land of Assyria is referred to as the land of Nimrod (<ref="Mic.5.6">Mic.5.6</ref>), further emphasizing his influence and power in the region.

entries.name: Noah
entries.brief: Righteous man, built ark, survived flood
entries.short: Noah was a righteous man who built the ark and survived the great flood with his family.
entries.article: Noah was the son of Lamech, a descendant of Seth (<ref="Gen.5.29-30">Gen.5.29-30</ref>). He was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked faithfully with God (<ref="Gen.6.9">Gen.6.9</ref>). When God saw the wickedness of humanity, He chose Noah to build an ark to save his family and representatives of all animals from the coming flood (<ref="Gen.6.13-22">Gen.6.13-22</ref>). Noah obeyed God and built the ark, and he and his family entered it along with the animals (Genesis 7). After the flood, Noah built an altar and made sacrifices to God (<ref="Gen.8.20">Gen.8.20</ref>). God blessed Noah and his sons, establishing a covenant with them and setting the rainbow as a sign of His promise never to destroy the earth by flood again (Genesis 9). Noah lived for 950 years (<ref="Gen.9.29">Gen.9.29</ref>). He is remembered as an example of faith (<ref="Heb.11.7">Heb.11.7</ref>) and righteousness (<ref="Ezk.14.14, 20">Ezk.14.14, 20</ref>; <ref="2Pe.2.5">2Pe.2.5</ref>).

entries.name: Oholibamah
entries.brief: Wife of Esau
entries.short: Oholibamah was one of Esau's wives, a descendant of Seir the Horite.
entries.article: Oholibamah was one of the wives of Esau, the son of Isaac and Rebekah (<ref="Gen.36.2">Gen.36.2</ref>). She was the daughter of Anah and the granddaughter of Zibeon, both descendants of Seir the Horite (<ref="Gen.36.2, 14">Gen.36.2, 14</ref>). Oholibamah bore three sons to Esau: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah (<ref="Gen.36.5, 14, 18">Gen.36.5, 14, 18</ref>). She is mentioned in the genealogies of Esau, which list his wives, descendants, and the chiefs of Edom (<ref="Gen.36.18, 41">Gen.36.18, 41</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.52">1Ch.1.52</ref>). As one of Esau's wives, Oholibamah played a role in the establishment of the Edomite nation, which descended from Esau.

entries.name: Omar
entries.brief: Son of Eliphaz, grandson of Esau
entries.short: Omar was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau, mentioned in the genealogies of Edom.
entries.article: Omar was one of the sons of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau (<ref="Gen.36.11, 15">Gen.36.11, 15</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.36">1Ch.1.36</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogies of Esau, which list the descendants of Esau and the chiefs of Edom. As a grandson of Esau, Omar was part of the Edomite clan and likely held a position of influence within the tribe.

entries.name: Onam
entries.brief: Descendant of Seir the Horite
entries.short: Onam was a descendant of Seir the Horite, mentioned in the genealogies of Edom.
entries.article: Onam was a descendant of Seir the Horite, a group that inhabited the land of Edom before Esau's descendants (<ref="Gen.36.23">Gen.36.23</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.40">1Ch.1.40</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogies of the Horites, which are recorded in the context of Esau's family history. The Horites were a people group that lived in the region of Seir, which later became known as Edom. Onam's mention in these genealogies suggests that he was a significant figure among the Horites.

entries.name: Ophir
entries.brief: Son of Joktan
entries.short: Ophir was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem, mentioned in the Table of Nations.
entries.article: Ophir was one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber (<ref="Gen.10.29">Gen.10.29</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.23">1Ch.1.23</ref>). He is mentioned in the Table of Nations, which lists the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Joktan's descendants, including Ophir, are said to have settled in the region "from Mesha all the way to Sephar, the eastern hill country" (<ref="Gen.10.30">Gen.10.30</ref>). The exact location of this region is uncertain, but it is generally believed to be in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. The name Ophir is also associated with a land famous for its wealth and gold (e.g., <ref="1Ki.9.28; 10.11; 22.48">1Ki.9.28; 10.11; 22.48</ref>; <ref="1Ch.29.4">1Ch.29.4</ref>; <ref="2Ch.8.18; 9.10">2Ch.8.18; 9.10</ref>; <ref="Job.22.24; 28.16">Job.22.24; 28.16</ref>; Psalm <ref="Job.45.9">Job.45.9</ref>; <ref="Isa.13.12">Isa.13.12</ref>), but it is unclear if this land was named after Joktan's son or another individual.

entries.name: Pathrusim
entries.brief: Descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham
entries.short: Pathrusim, a People from Mizraim, son of Ham, according to <ref="Genesis 10:14">Genesis 10:14</ref>.
entries.article: The Pathrusim were a people group listed among the descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham, in <ref="Gen.10.14">Gen.10.14</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.12">1Ch.1.12</ref>. Mizraim was the ancestor of the Egyptians and other related peoples. The Pathrusim are mentioned only in these genealogical lists and are not referred to elsewhere in the Bible. They were probably inhabitants of the region of Pathros in Upper Egypt, which is mentioned several times in the prophets as a place where Jews had settled (<ref="Isa.11.11">Isa.11.11</ref>; <ref="Jer.44.1,15">Jer.44.1,15</ref>; <ref="Ezk.29.14; 30.14">Ezk.29.14; 30.14</ref>).

entries.name: Peleg
entries.brief: Descendant of Shem, ancestor of Abraham
entries.short: Peleg, a descendant of Shem and ancestor of Abraham, during whose time the earth was divided.
entries.article: Peleg was a descendant of Shem, the son of Noah, and an ancestor of Abraham, according to the genealogies in <ref="Gen.10.25, 11">Gen.10.25, 11</ref>:16-19, and <ref="1Ch.1.19,25">1Ch.1.19,25</ref>. He was the son of Eber and the brother of Joktan. Peleg lived 239 years and became the father of Reu at the age of 30. The name Peleg means "division," and <ref="Gen.10.25">Gen.10.25</ref> states that in his days the earth was divided. This event is not described in detail, but it may refer to the division of languages and peoples described in the Tower of Babel story (<ref="Gen.11.1-9">Gen.11.1-9</ref>). Peleg is also mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in <ref="Luk.3.35">Luk.3.35</ref>, emphasizing his role in the ancestral line of the Messiah.

entries.name: Philistine
entries.brief: Descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham
entries.short: The Philistines, a people group descended from Mizraim, the son of Ham, according to the Table of Nations in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: The Philistines are mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis 10 and 1Chronicles 1, which record the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. In these passages, the Philistines are listed as descendants of Mizraim, the son of Ham (<ref="Gen.10.14">Gen.10.14</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.12">1Ch.1.12</ref>). This suggests that the Philistines were related to the Egyptians and other Hamitic peoples. The Table of Nations provides a general overview of the geographic distribution and ethnic relationships of the ancient world, but it does not give specific details about the Philistines' history or culture. Throughout the Old Testament, the Philistines are portrayed as one of the main enemies of Israel, occupying the coastal plain of Canaan and engaging in numerous conflicts with the Israelites during the period of the judges and the early monarchy.

entries.name: Pinon
entries.brief: Edomite clan chief descended from Esau
entries.short: Pinon, one of the chiefs of Edom, descended from Esau, mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Pinon is mentioned in the genealogies of Esau in <ref="Gen.36.41">Gen.36.41</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.52">1Ch.1.52</ref> as one of the chiefs of Edom. He is listed among the descendants of Esau, who was the son of Isaac and the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob'). The Edomites, descended from Esau, settled in the region south of the Dead Sea, which became known as the land of Edom. Pinon's mention in these genealogies suggests that he was a significant leader or clan head among the Edomites. However, no further details are provided about his life, achievements, or the specific clan he led.

entries.name: Put
entries.brief: Son of Ham, grandson of Noah
entries.short: Put was a son of Ham and grandson of Noah.
entries.article: Put was one of the sons of Ham, who was a son of Noah (<ref="Gen.10.6">Gen.10.6</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.8">1Ch.1.8</ref>). He was born after the Great Flood and was a brother to Cush, Mizraim (Egypt), and Canaan. The descendants of Put are not explicitly mentioned in the Bible, but his name is often associated with the region of Libya or the Libyan people. Some ancient historians and geographers, such as Josephus and Pliny the Elder, connected Put with Libya. In some Bible translations, the name Put is rendered as Libya or Libyans in passages such as <ref="Ezk.27.10">Ezk.27.10</ref> and <ref="Nam.3.9">Nam.3.9</ref>, where it appears in the context of nations that had trade relations with Tyre or were part of the Assyrian army.

entries.name: Raamah
entries.brief: Son of Cush, grandson of Ham, great-grandson of Noah
entries.short: Raamah was a son of Cush, grandson of Ham, and great-grandson of Noah, mentioned in the Table of Nations.
entries.article: Raamah is mentioned in the genealogy of the nations in Genesis 10, also known as the Table of Nations (<ref="Gen.10.7">Gen.10.7</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.9">1Ch.1.9</ref>). He was a son of Cush, who was a son of Ham, making Raamah a grandson of Ham and a great-grandson of Noah. The Table of Nations records the descendants of Noah's sons and their dispersal after the Tower of Babel. Raamah's sons, Sheba and Dedan, are also mentioned, suggesting that they became ancestors of tribes or nations. Some scholars associate Raamah with a region in southern Arabia, based on the connection with Sheba and Dedan, which are often linked to Arabian tribes. However, the exact location and identity of Raamah and his descendants remain uncertain.

entries.name: Reu
entries.brief: Son of Peleg, ancestor of Abraham
entries.short: Reu was the son of Peleg and an ancestor of Abraham, living to the age of 239 years.
entries.article: Reu, mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis 11, 1Chronicles 1, and Luke 3, was the son of Peleg and an ancestor of Abraham. He was born when Peleg was 30 years old (<ref="Gen.11.18">Gen.11.18</ref>) and lived for a total of 239 years (<ref="Gen.11.20-21">Gen.11.20-21</ref>). Reu fathered Serug at the age of 32 and lived an additional 207 years, having other sons and daughters (<ref="Gen.11.19-21">Gen.11.19-21</ref>). He is listed as one of the descendants of Shem, the son of Noah, and is part of the lineage that traces from Adam to Abraham, and ultimately to Jesus Christ (<ref="Luk.3.35">Luk.3.35</ref>). The name Reu means "friend" or "associate" in Hebrew. His inclusion in the genealogies emphasizes the continuity of the godly line from which the Messiah would eventually come.

entries.name: Reuel
entries.brief: Son of Esau and Basemath, a chief of Edom
entries.short: Reuel was a son of Esau and Basemath, and he became a chief in the land of Edom.
entries.article: Reuel was one of the sons of Esau, Jacob's brother, and Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael (<ref="Gen.36.4, 10, 13, 17">Gen.36.4, 10, 13, 17</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.35, 37">1Ch.1.35, 37</ref>). He was born in Canaan before Esau moved his family to the hill country of Seir, which later became known as Edom (<ref="Gen.36.8-9">Gen.36.8-9</ref>). Reuel became one of the chiefs of Edom, indicating that he held a position of authority and influence among the Edomites (<ref="Gen.36.17">Gen.36.17</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.37">1Ch.1.37</ref>). His sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah (<ref="Gen.36.13, 17">Gen.36.13, 17</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.37">1Ch.1.37</ref>). The Edomites, descendants of Esau, lived in the region south of the Dead Sea and were often in conflict with the Israelites throughout their history. The mention of Reuel and his descendants in the genealogies of Esau demonstrates the fulfillment of God's promise to make Esau into a nation (<ref="Gen.25.23">Gen.25.23</ref>) and provides insight into the early history and leadership of the Edomites.

entries.name: Sabteca
entries.brief: Son of Cush, grandson of Ham
entries.short: Sabteca was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, mentioned in the Table of Nations.
entries.article: Sabteca is mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.7">Gen.10.7</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.9">1Ch.1.9</ref> as one of the sons of Cush, who was a son of Ham. He is listed among the descendants of Noah's sons in the Table of Nations, which records the dispersal of people groups after the Flood (<ref="Gen.10.1-32">Gen.10.1-32</ref>). The precise identity and location of the People from Sabteca are unknown, but some scholars suggest a connection with the ancient city of Samydake, mentioned by Greek geographer Strabo, which was located on the southern coast of the Arabian Peninsula. Others propose a link with the ancient kingdom of Sabata, located in the same region. However, these associations remain speculative due to the limited information provided in the biblical text. The inclusion of Sabteca in the Table of Nations highlights the diversity of peoples and nations that emerged from the descendants of Noah and their spread across the earth after the Flood.

entries.name: Samlah
entries.brief: King of Edom before Israel had kings
entries.short: Samlah was a king of Edom who reigned before Israel had kings, as mentioned in the genealogies of Esau.
entries.article: Samlah is mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.36-37">Gen.36.36-37</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.47-48">1Ch.1.47-48</ref> as one of the kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had kings. He was from the city of Masrekah and succeeded Hadad, son of Bedad, as king of Edom. After Samlah's death, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River succeeded him as king. The genealogies in Genesis 36 and 1Chronicles 1 list the descendants of Esau, who was Jacob's brother, and the kings who ruled in Edom. These kings were not necessarily related to each other, and their reigns were not dynastic. The mention of these kings demonstrates Edom's political organization and its existence as a nation before Israel had a centralized monarchy. Samlah's inclusion in these lists provides a glimpse into the history of Edom and its relationship with Israel.

entries.name: Seba
entries.brief: Son of Cush, brother of Raamah
entries.short: Seba was a son of Cush and brother of Raamah.
entries.article: Seba is mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.7">Gen.10.7</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.9">1Ch.1.9</ref> as a son of Cush and a brother of Raamah. He is listed among the descendants of Ham, one of Noah's sons, in the Table of Nations. The Table of Nations in Genesis 10 provides a genealogical record of the repopulation of the earth after the Flood. Seba and his relatives are associated with the southern Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa region. Although little is known about Seba as an individual, his mention in the genealogy suggests that he was a significant ancestor of a people group or region.

entries.name: Seir
entries.brief: Horite chief, ancestor of the Horites of Seir
entries.short: Seir was a Horite chief and an ancestor of the Horites who inhabited the land of Seir.
entries.article: Seir is mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.20-21">Gen.36.20-21</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.38">1Ch.1.38</ref> as a Horite chief and an ancestor of the Horites who inhabited the land of Seir. The Horites were the original inhabitants of the region of Seir before the descendants of Esau settled there. Seir is listed among the sons of Seir the Horite, indicating that he was a prominent figure among the Horite clans. The land of Seir, located in the region of Edom, south of the Dead Sea, was named after Seir the Horite. The descendants of Esau, also known as the Edomites, later inhabited this region and intermarried with the Horites.

entries.name: Serug
entries.brief: Son of Reu; father of Nahor, ancestor of Abraham
entries.short: Serug was the son of Reu, the father of Nahor, and an ancestor of Abraham, living to the age of 230 years.
entries.article: Serug, mentioned in <ref="Gen.11.20-23, 1">Gen.11.20-23, 1</ref> Chronicles <ref="Gen.1.26">Gen.1.26</ref>, and <ref="Luk.3.35">Luk.3.35</ref>, was a descendant of Shem and an ancestor of Abraham. He was the son of Reu and the father of Nahor. Serug lived 30 years before becoming the father of Nahor, and after that, he lived an additional 200 years, having other sons and daughters. In total, Serug lived 230 years. He is listed in the genealogies that trace the lineage from Shem to Abraham, highlighting the continuity of God's plan through the generations. Serug's mention in both the Old and New Testaments underscores the importance of family lineage in the biblical narrative.

entries.name: Seth
entries.brief: Third son of Adam and Eve, ancestor of righteous line
entries.short: Seth was the third son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel, and became the ancestor of the righteous line of humanity.
entries.article: Seth, mentioned in <ref="Gen.4.25-26, 5">Gen.4.25-26, 5</ref>:3-8, <ref="1Ch.1.1">1Ch.1.1</ref>, <ref="Num.24.17">Num.24.17</ref>, and <ref="Luk.3.38">Luk.3.38</ref>, was the third son of Adam and Eve. He was born after the death of Abel, whom Cain had murdered. Eve named him Seth, saying, "God has appointed me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him." Seth became the ancestor of the righteous line of humanity, in contrast to Cain's descendants. When Seth was 105 years old, he became the father of Enosh, and he lived an additional 807 years, having other sons and daughters. In total, Seth lived 912 years. His descendants, including Enoch and Noah, are characterized as calling upon the name of the Lord. In <ref="Num.24.17">Num.24.17</ref>, the oracle of Balaam refers to a star coming out of Israel (or 'Jacob') and a scepter rising out of Israel, which some interpret as a reference to the Messiah descending from Seth's lineage. Seth's inclusion in the genealogy of Jesus in <ref="Luk.3.38">Luk.3.38</ref> further emphasizes his significance in the biblical narrative.

entries.name: Shammah
entries.brief: Son of Reuel, grandson of Esau
entries.short: Shammah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau, and he became a chief of Edom.
entries.article: Shammah, mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.13,17">Gen.36.13,17</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.37">1Ch.1.37</ref>, was a descendant of Esau, the twin brother of Israel (or 'Jacob'). He was the son of Reuel, who was one of Esau's sons. Shammah is listed among the chiefs of Edom, indicating that he held a position of authority and leadership within the Edomite tribe. The Edomites were descendants of Esau who settled in the region southeast of Judah. The text does not provide any specific details about Shammah's life or his role as a chief. However, his inclusion in the genealogical record of Esau's descendants highlights the importance of family lineage and the development of tribal structures in the ancient Near East. The mention of Shammah as a chief suggests that he played a significant role in the political and social organization of the Edomites.

entries.name: Sheba
entries.brief: Descendant of Joktan, settling in southern Arabia
entries.short: Sheba, a descendant of Joktan, is associated with the ancient kingdom of Sheba in southern Arabia, known for its wealth and trade.
entries.article: Sheba, mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.28">Gen.10.28</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.22">1Ch.1.22</ref>, was a descendant of Joktan, who was a descendant of Shem, one of Noah's sons. Joktan's descendants are associated with the peoples and tribes of southern Arabia. Sheba, in particular, is linked to the ancient kingdom of Sheba, located in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, in modern-day Yemen. The Sabeans, the inhabitants of Sheba, were renowned for their wealth, trade in spices, gold, and precious stones, and their influential position in the ancient Near Eastern trade network. The connection between Sheba, the descendant of Joktan, and the kingdom of Sheba suggests that the Joktanites may have been among the early settlers and founders of this prosperous kingdom. The mention of Sheba in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10) and the genealogy in 1 Chronicles highlights the spread and distribution of the descendants of Noah's sons after the Flood and their role in populating various regions of the ancient world.

entries.name: Shelah
entries.brief: Son of Arpachshad and ancestor of Abraham
entries.short: Shelah, son of Arpachshad and ancestor of Abraham in Luke's genealogy.
entries.article:
Shelah was the son of Arpachshad (or Arphaxad) and the grandson of Shem, according to <ref="Gen.10.24">Gen.10.24</ref> and <ref="Gen.11.12">Gen.11.12</ref>. He was born when Arpachshad was 35 years old and lived for 433 years (<ref="Gen.11.12-15">Gen.11.12-15</ref>). Shelah was an ancestor of Abraham and is included in the genealogies of Genesis 10, 11, and 1Chronicles 1. 

In Luke's genealogy of Jesus, Shelah is mentioned as the son of Cainan, who was the son of Arpachshad (<ref="Luk.3.35-36">Luk.3.35-36</ref>). This differs from the Old Testament genealogies, which list Shelah as the son of Arpachshad. The reason for this discrepancy is uncertain, but it may reflect variant traditions or textual issues.

entries.name: Sheleph
entries.brief: Son of Joktan, descendant of Shem
entries.short: Sheleph, a son of Joktan and descendant of Shem.
entries.article: Sheleph was one of the sons of Joktan, who was a descendant of Shem, according to <ref="Gen.10.26">Gen.10.26</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.20">1Ch.1.20</ref>. He is mentioned in the genealogies of the nations descended from Noah's sons after the flood. The descendants of Joktan, including Sheleph, are listed as living in the region from Mesha to Sephar, in the eastern hill country.

entries.name: Shem
entries.brief: Noah's son, ancestor of Semitic peoples
entries.short: Shem, one of Noah's three sons and the ancestor of the Semitic peoples.
entries.article:
Shem was one of the three sons of Noah, along with Ham and Japheth (<ref="Gen.5.32; 6.10">Gen.5.32; 6.10</ref>). He and his wife were among the eight people who survived the great flood in the ark (<ref="Gen.7.13">Gen.7.13</ref>). After the flood, Shem and his brothers became the ancestors of the nations that repopulated the earth (<ref="Gen.9.18,19; 10.1">Gen.9.18,19; 10.1</ref>). 

Shem was the ancestor of the Semitic peoples, including the Elamites, Assyrians, Arameans, and Hebrews (<ref="Gen.10.21-31">Gen.10.21-31</ref>). He was also the ancestor of Abraham and, therefore, of the Israelites (<ref="Gen.11.10-26">Gen.11.10-26</ref>; <ref="1Ch.1.17-27">1Ch.1.17-27</ref>). In the New Testament, Shem is mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in <ref="Luk.3.36">Luk.3.36</ref>. 

Shem and Japheth showed respect for their father by covering his nakedness when he became drunk (<ref="Gen.9.23">Gen.9.23</ref>). As a result, Noah blessed Shem, saying, "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem" (<ref="Gen.9.26">Gen.9.26</ref>). This blessing implied that Shem's descendants would have a special relationship with God. Shem lived for 600 years (<ref="Gen.11.10-11">Gen.11.10-11</ref>).

entries.name: Shepho
entries.brief: Horite chief, son of Shobal
entries.short: Shepho, a Horite chief, the son of Shobal, who lived in the land of Seir.
entries.article: Shepho was a Horite chief mentioned in <ref="1Ch.1.40">1Ch.1.40</ref> and <ref="Gen.36.23">Gen.36.23</ref>. He was the son of Shobal and lived in the land of Seir, which was later inhabited by the Edomites. The Horites were the original inhabitants of Seir before the descendants of Esau (the Edomites) displaced them. Shepho is listed among the chiefs of the Horites, indicating his position of authority within their tribal structure. These genealogical records provide insight into the early inhabitants of the region and their leadership.

entries.name: Shobal
entries.brief: Horite chief, son of Seir, in the land of Edom.
entries.short: Shobal was a Horite chief, the son of Seir, who lived in the land of Edom.
entries.article: Shobal is mentioned in <ref="Gen.36.20,23,29">Gen.36.20,23,29</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.38,40">1Ch.1.38,40</ref> as one of the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land of Edom before the descendants of Esau. Shobal is described as a Horite chief, indicating his leadership position within the Horite clan. The Horites were the original inhabitants of the mountainous region of Seir, which later became known as Edom. Shobal's descendants, along with the other Horite clans, are listed in the genealogy of the chiefs of Edom. This genealogy demonstrates the intermingling of the Horites with the Edomites, who were descended from Esau, and the eventual dominance of the Edomites in the region.

entries.name: Shuah
entries.brief: Son of Abraham and Keturah, ancestor of a tribe.
entries.short: Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah, and his descendants formed a tribe.
entries.article: Shuah is mentioned in <ref="Gen.25.2">Gen.25.2</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.32">1Ch.1.32</ref> as one of the sons of Abraham and his second wife, Keturah. After the death of Sarah, Abraham took Keturah as his wife, and she bore him six sons, including Shuah. These sons were sent away with gifts to the east, away from Abraham's son Isaac, to whom he gave his main inheritance. Shuah's descendants formed a tribe, although no further details about their history or location are provided in the biblical text. The mention of Shuah and his brothers demonstrates Abraham's fulfillment of God's promise to make him the father of many nations, even though the covenant was primarily established through his son Isaac.

entries.name: Sidon
entries.brief: Firstborn son of Canaan, ancestor of the Sidonians.
entries.short: Sidon was the firstborn son of Canaan and the ancestor of the Sidonian people.
entries.article: Sidon is mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.15">Gen.10.15</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.13">1Ch.1.13</ref> as the firstborn son of Canaan, who was the son of Ham and the grandson of Noah. Sidon is listed among the descendants of Canaan, along with his brothers Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, and others. The descendants of Canaan inhabited the region that later became known as Canaan, which included the cities of Sidon and Tyre. The Sidonians, who were descended from Sidon, became known for their maritime trade and their skilled craftsmanship, particularly in the production of purple dye and glass. The city of Sidon, named after its ancestor, became one of the most important Phoenician cities and is frequently mentioned in the Bible as a center of commerce and culture.

entries.name: Sinites
entries.brief: Canaanite people group descended from Canaan.
entries.short: The Sinites were a Canaanite people group descended from Canaan, the son of Ham.
entries.article: The Sinites are mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.17">Gen.10.17</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.15">1Ch.1.15</ref> as one of the descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham and grandson of Noah. They are listed among the Canaanite tribes, which also included the Sidonians, Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, and others. The Sinites were part of the people groups that inhabited the land of Canaan before the Israelites' arrival. The exact location of their territory is not specified in the Bible, and little is known about their culture or history. As Canaanites, they were among the people groups that God promised to drive out of the land to give to the Israelites (<ref="Exo.23.23">Exo.23.23</ref>; <ref="Deu.7.1">Deu.7.1</ref>). The mention of the Sinites in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10) and the genealogy of Chronicles serves to highlight the diverse people groups that descended from Noah's sons and populated the ancient Near East.

entries.name: Tarshish
entries.brief: Son of Javan, great-grandson of Noah
entries.short: Tarshish was a son of Javan and great-grandson of Noah, associated with the ancient city of Tarshish.
entries.article: Tarshish is mentioned in <ref="Gen.10.4">Gen.10.4</ref> and <ref="1Ch.1.7">1Ch.1.7</ref> as a son of Javan and grandson of Noah.
