In Jacob's blessing, Issachar was described as a "strong donkey" and "resting between the sheepfolds", indicating his tribe would be hardworking and content with an agrarian life (Gen. 49:14-15). 

During the wilderness years, the tribe of Issachar was led by Nethanel son of Zuar (Num. 1:8; 2:5; 7:18; 10:15). They encamped on the east side of the tabernacle under the standard of Judah (Num. 2:5). 

In the census taken in the wilderness of Sinai, the tribe of Issachar numbered 54,400 men aged 20 and over (Num. 1:28-29). In the second census on the plains of Moab they numbered 64,300 (Num. 26:25). 

Issachar's allotment in Canaan included the fertile Jezreel Valley and was bordered by Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Jordan (Josh. 19:17-23). The Levitical cities in Issachar's territory were Kishion, Daberath, Jarmuth and En-gannim (Josh. 21:28-29). 

The tribe of Issachar was commended for providing wise leadership during the time of David (1Chr. 12:32). One of David's officers, Omri son of Michael, was from Issachar (1Chr. 27:18). The tribe is also noted for being faithful to Hezekiah's Passover invitation (2Chr. 30:18). 

In Ezekiel's vision of the division of the restored land, Issachar is allotted the sixth portion (Ezek. 48:25-26). In John's apocalyptic vision, Issachar is one of the tribes sealed by God (Rev. 7:7).

entries.name: Ithrites
entries.brief: Clan descended from Kiriath-jearim; two of David's warriors.
entries.short: The Ithrites were a clan descended from Kiriath-jearim (<ref="1Ch.2.53">1Ch.2.53</ref>), and two of David's mighty warriors, Ira and Gareb, were Ithrites.
entries.article:
The Ithrites were a clan or family group mentioned in the Bible, descended from the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, a town in Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.53">1Ch.2.53</ref>). Kiriath-jearim was one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah (<ref="Jos.15.60">Jos.15.60</ref>) and was the place where the ark of the covenant was kept for a time before being brought to Jerusalem by David (<ref="1Sa.7.1-2">1Sa.7.1-2</ref>; <ref="2Sa.6.2-4">2Sa.6.2-4</ref>). 

Two of David's mighty warriors, Ira and Gareb, are identified as Ithrites (<ref="2Sa.23.38">2Sa.23.38</ref>; <ref="1Ch.11.40">1Ch.11.40</ref>). These men were part of an elite group of soldiers who served David faithfully and were renowned for their military prowess (<ref="2Sa.23.8-39">2Sa.23.8-39</ref>; <ref="1Ch.11.10-47">1Ch.11.10-47</ref>). 

The mention of the Ithrites in these passages highlights the importance of family and clan connections in Israelite society and the role that certain groups played in the military and political life of the nation. It also demonstrates the significance of Kiriath-jearim as a town with a rich history and connection to the ark of the covenant.

entries.name: Jada
entries.brief: Son of Onam and brother of Shammai.
entries.short: Jada was the son of Onam and the brother of Shammai, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article:
Jada is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.28">1Ch.2.28</ref> and 32 as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is identified as the son of Onam and the brother of Shammai. 

The genealogy in this chapter traces the descendants of Judah, one of the twelve sons of Israel (or 'Jacob'). It provides a detailed record of the families and clans within the tribe of Judah, highlighting significant individuals and their relationships. 

Jada's father, Onam, is listed as a descendant of Jerahmeel, who was one of the sons of Hezron, a grandson of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.25">1Ch.2.25</ref>). This places Jada within the larger context of the Jerahmeelite clan within the tribe of Judah. 

Apart from his familial connections, no other specific details are provided about Jada's life, occupation, or role within the tribe. His inclusion in the genealogy serves to maintain a record of the lineage of Judah and to demonstrate the continuity of the tribe through successive generations. 

The preservation of such genealogical records was important for the Israelites, as it helped to establish tribal identity, inheritance rights, and the fulfillment of God's promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

entries.name: Jahdai
entries.brief: Descendant of Caleb, son of Jephunneh.
entries.short: Jahdai was one of the descendants of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh.
entries.article:
Jahdai is mentioned briefly in <ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref> as one of the descendants of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh. This passage is part of a larger genealogical record of the tribe of Judah, focusing particularly on the descendants of Hezron, one of the sons of Perez (<ref="1Ch.2.3-55">1Ch.2.3-55</ref>). 

Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, is known for his faithfulness to the Lord during the time of the Israelites' wandering in the wilderness (<ref="Num.14.24">Num.14.24</ref>, <ref="Jos.14.6-14">Jos.14.6-14</ref>). He was one of the twelve spies sent to explore the land of Canaan, and along with Joshua, he brought back a positive report and encouraged the people to trust in the Lord (<ref="Num.13.30, 14">Num.13.30, 14</ref>.6-9). 

In 1Chronicles 2, several of Caleb's descendants are listed, including his sons and grandsons. Jahdai is mentioned among these descendants (<ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>), indicating that he was part of Caleb's lineage and a member of the tribe of Judah. 

No other specific details are provided about Jahdai's life, occupation, or role within the family or tribe. His inclusion in this genealogical record, however, serves to highlight the importance of family lineage and the preservation of ancestral records among the Israelites, particularly within the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Jair
entries.brief: Manassite leader who captured Gilead
entries.short: Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, captured the region of Gilead.
entries.article: Jair was a descendant of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, who played a significant role in the conquest and settlement of the region east of the Jordan River. According to <ref="Num.32.41">Num.32.41</ref> and <ref="Deu.3.14">Deu.3.14</ref>, Jair captured the settlements in Gilead and named them Havvoth-jair, which means "the towns of Jair." <ref="1Ch.2.22">1Ch.2.22</ref> states that Jair controlled twenty-three cities in Gilead. In <ref="2Sa.20.26">2Sa.20.26</ref>, a person named Ira the Jairite is mentioned as one of David's officials, possibly indicating that Jair's descendants continued to hold influential positions. <ref="1Ki.4.13">1Ki.4.13</ref> refers to the towns of Jair in the context of Solomon's administrative districts, suggesting that the region remained associated with Jair's name long after his lifetime.

entries.name: Jamin
entries.brief: Son of Ram, descendant of Judah
entries.short: Jamin was a son of Ram and a descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Jamin is briefly mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.27">1Ch.2.27</ref> as one of the sons of Ram, along with his brothers Bunah, Oren, and Ozem. Ram was a descendant of Judah through Hezron and Jerahmeel. The genealogy in this chapter traces the lineage of Judah, focusing on the descendants of Hezron. No further information is provided about Jamin's life or his role within the tribe of Judah. His mention in the genealogy suggests that he was an ancestor of some of the families within the tribe, although no specific details are given about his descendants.

entries.name: Jarha
entries.brief: Egyptian servant who married Sheshan's daughter
entries.short: Jarha was an Egyptian servant who married the daughter of Sheshan, a descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Jarha is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.34-35">1Ch.2.34-35</ref> as an Egyptian servant who married the daughter of Sheshan, a descendant of Judah. Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, so he gave one of his daughters in marriage to his servant Jarha. This marriage between an Israelite woman and an Egyptian servant was unusual, as it deviated from the typical practice of marrying within one's tribe or nation. The text does not provide any further details about Jarha's life or his relationship with Sheshan's daughter. However, their marriage resulted in the continuation of Sheshan's lineage, as Jarha's son Attai is listed among the descendants of Judah. This inclusion of Jarha in the genealogy of Judah demonstrates that God's plan can work through unexpected means and that one's background does not limit their potential to be part of God's people.

entries.name: Jehu
entries.brief: Son of Obed, a descendant of Judah.
entries.short: Jehu was a descendant of Judah through Obed, as recorded in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jehu, the son of Obed, is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles. He was a descendant of Hezron, one of the sons of Perez, who was a son of Judah.

entries.name: Jekamiah
entries.brief: Son of Shallum, a descendant of Judah.
entries.short: Jekamiah was a descendant of Judah through Shallum, as recorded in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jekamiah is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Shallum, who was a descendant of Sheshan, from the clan of Jerahmeel. The genealogy traces Jekamiah's lineage back to Judah, one of the twelve sons of Israel (or 'Jacob').

entries.name: Jerahmeel
entries.brief: Son of Hezron, a descendant of Judah.
entries.short: Jerahmeel was the son of Hezron and a prominent figure in the genealogy of Judah, with his descendants being called the Jerahmeelites.
entries.article: Jerahmeel was the son of Hezron, a descendant of Judah, and is mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He had two wives, Atarah and Ahijah, and several children who became the founders of various clans within the tribe of Judah. Jerahmeel's descendants, known as the Jerahmeelites, are mentioned in connection with David's time as a fugitive from King Saul. David sent gifts to the Jerahmeelites, among others, after defeating the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. This suggests that the Jerahmeelites were a significant clan within Judah and had a friendly relationship with David. The Jerahmeelites' territory was likely located in the Negev region, south of Judah.

entries.name: Jerioth
entries.brief: Wife of Caleb; mother of unnamed children.
entries.short: Jerioth was one of the wives of Caleb, and she bore him some unnamed children, as mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jerioth is mentioned briefly in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles as one of the wives of Caleb, the son of Hezron. The passage states that Caleb had children by his wife Azubah, and after her death, he married Ephrath. It then mentions that Caleb also had children by Jerioth. The wording at 1Chr <ref="2.18">2.18</ref> makes it possible this was another name for Azubah who had Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.

entries.name: Jesher
entries.brief: A son of Caleb and Azubah.
entries.short: Jesher was one of the sons of Caleb and his wife Azubah, as mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jesher is mentioned briefly in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Caleb and his wife Azubah. The passage states that Caleb had children by his wife Azubah, and after her death, he married Ephrath. It then lists Jesher, along with his brothers Shobab and Ardon, as the sons of Caleb and Azubah.

entries.name: Jesse
entries.brief: Father of King David.
entries.short: Jesse was the father of King David and an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
entries.article: Jesse was a Bethlehemite from the tribe of Judah and the father of King David. He is first mentioned in the book of Ruth as the son of Obed and the grandson of Boaz and Ruth. Jesse had eight sons, the youngest of whom was David, who was anointed by the prophet Samuel to be king over Israel. Jesse is described as an old man during the time of David's youth, and he sent David to take supplies to his older brothers who were fighting in Saul's army against the Philistines. Later, when David was on the run from Saul, he expressed concern for his parents' safety, and he arranged for them to stay with the king of Moab. Jesse is also mentioned in the genealogies of Jesus Christ in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, emphasizing the Messianic lineage from Jesse through David. The prophet Isaiah foretold that the Messiah would come from the "stump of Jesse," symbolizing the humble origins of the Davidic dynasty.

entries.name: Jether
entries.brief: A son of Jada from the tribe of Judah.
entries.short: Jether was a son of Jada, a descendant of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles.
entries.article: Jether is mentioned briefly in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles. He is listed as one of the sons of Jada within the tribe of Judah. The genealogies in Chronicles serve to establish the lineage and heritage of important figures in Israel's history and to demonstrate God's faithfulness to His promises through the generations.

entries.name: Joab
entries.brief: Son of Zeruiah, commander of David's army
entries.short: Joab, David's nephew and commander of his army, was a key figure in David's reign, known for his military prowess and loyalty.
entries.article:
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was King David's nephew and the commander of his army. He first appears in <ref="1Sa.26.6">1Sa.26.6</ref>, accompanying David on a mission to Saul's camp. Joab played a significant role in David's rise to power and the establishment of his kingdom (2Sa.2-3; 8.16; <ref="1Ch.11.6,8">1Ch.11.6,8</ref>). 

As a military commander, Joab led David's forces in various battles against the Ammonites, Syrians, and other enemies (2Sa.10; 12.26-27; 1Ch.19). He also helped quell Absalom's rebellion and was instrumental in defeating Sheba's revolt (2Sa.18; 20). 

However, Joab's loyalty to David was sometimes overshadowed by his own ambition and ruthlessness. He killed Abner, Saul's former commander, in revenge for his brother Asahel's death (2Sa.3). He also disobeyed David's orders by killing Absalom (2Sa.18) and supported Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne (<ref="1Ki.1.7,19">1Ki.1.7,19</ref>). 

Despite his flaws, Joab remained a key figure in David's reign until the end. He was involved in the census that brought God's judgment upon Israel (2Sa.24; 1Ch.21) and was eventually killed by Benaiah on Solomon's orders for his support of Adonijah (<ref="1Ki.2.28-35">1Ki.2.28-35</ref>).

entries.name: Jonathan
entries.brief: Son of Jada, descendant of Judah
entries.short: One of the descendants of Judah, Jonathan was the son of Jada.
entries.article: Jonathan was a descendant of Judah, the son of Jada and brother of Jether. He is mentioned in the genealogies of Judah recorded in <ref="1Ch.2.32-33">1Ch.2.32-33</ref>. No other details are provided about his life. His mention helps trace Judah's descendants down to the time period after the return from Babylonian exile when Chronicles was likely written.

entries.name: Jorkeam
entries.brief: A son or town founded by Raham
entries.short: Jorkeam was a descendant of Caleb or a town founded by Raham in the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Jorkeam is mentioned briefly in <ref="1Ch.2.44">1Ch.2.44</ref> as one of the descendants of Caleb or a town founded by Raham his 'father'. Caleb was from the tribe of Judah and is known for his faithfulness to God during the Israelites' wilderness wanderings (<ref="Num.13.30; 14.24">Num.13.30; 14.24</ref>). In the genealogy of Judah recorded in 1Chronicles 2, Jorkeam is listed as the son of Raham or the town founded by him.

entries.name: Joseph
entries.brief: Son of Jacob, ruler in Egypt
entries.short: Joseph, Jacob's son, rose to power in Egypt and saved his family during a famine.
entries.article: Joseph was the eleventh son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and the firstborn of Rachel (<ref="Gen.30.22-24">Gen.30.22-24</ref>). He was favored by his father, causing jealousy among his brothers (<ref="Gen.37.3-4">Gen.37.3-4</ref>). Joseph had dreams of his family bowing down to him, further straining the relationships (<ref="Gen.37.5-11">Gen.37.5-11</ref>). His brothers sold him into slavery, and he was taken to Egypt (<ref="Gen.37.12-36">Gen.37.12-36</ref>). In Egypt, Joseph served in Potiphar's house, where he was falsely accused and imprisoned (Genesis 39). While in prison, Joseph interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker (Genesis 40). Later, he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and was appointed as second-in-command over Egypt (<ref="Gen.41.1-45">Gen.41.1-45</ref>). During this time, he was given the name Zaphenath-paneah by Pharaoh (<ref="Gen.41.45">Gen.41.45</ref>). Joseph managed Egypt's resources wisely during the years of plenty and famine (<ref="Gen.41.46-57">Gen.41.46-57</ref>). His brothers came to Egypt for food, and after testing them, Joseph revealed his identity and reconciled with them (Genesis 42-45). Joseph brought his father, Jacob, and his entire family to Egypt, where they settled in the land of Goshen (Genesis 46-47). Before his death, Jacob blessed Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and prophesied about Joseph's descendants (Genesis 48-49). Joseph died at the age of 110 and was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt (<ref="Gen.50.22-26">Gen.50.22-26</ref>). His bones were later carried out of Egypt by the Israelites during the Exodus and buried at Shechem (<ref="Exo.13.19">Exo.13.19</ref>; <ref="Jos.24.32">Jos.24.32</ref>). Joseph's life exemplified faith, forgiveness, and God's providence in the midst of hardship.

entries.name: Jotham
entries.brief: A son of Jahdai, a Calebite
entries.short: Jotham was a son of Jahdai, who was a wife of Caleb.
entries.article:
Jotham is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref> as one of the sons of Jahdai. The context of the passage is the genealogy of Caleb, one of the leaders of the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.42-55">1Ch.2.42-55</ref>). 

Caleb's descendants are listed, including his great-grandson Jahdai (<ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>). Jotham is named as one of the six sons of Jahdai, along with Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph (<ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>). 

No further information is provided about Jotham's life, occupation, or role within the family or tribe. His mention serves to complete the genealogical record of Caleb's descendants.

entries.name: Judah
entries.brief: Israelite tribe, kingdom, and province
entries.short: Judah, also known as the Jews or Judea, refers to the Israelite tribe, the southern kingdom, and the Roman province in various biblical contexts.
entries.article:
Judah, Jews, and Judea are terms used throughout the Bible to refer to the Israelite tribe, the southern kingdom, and the Roman province, depending on the historical context. 

Judah was the fourth son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and Leah (<ref="Gen.29.35">Gen.29.35</ref>) and became the founder of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The tribe of Judah played a prominent role in Israel's history, with notable figures such as Caleb, Othniel, and King David coming from this tribe. 

After the reign of Solomon, the kingdom of Israel split into two: the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah (1Kings 12). The southern kingdom, which included the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, remained loyal to the Davidic dynasty and the worship of God in Jerusalem. The kingdom of Judah lasted from about 930 BC until the Babylonian conquest in 586 BC. 

Following the Babylonian exile, many Jews returned to the land of Judah, now a province of the Persian Empire (Ezra 1-6). During the Second Temple period, Judea became a province of the Roman Empire. In the New Testament, the terms "Jews" and "Judea" are often used to refer to the Jewish people and the region they inhabited. 

The history of Judah, the Jews, and Judea is a central focus of the biblical narrative, with many of the key events, prophecies, and teachings revolving around this people and their relationship with God. The prophets, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, often addressed their messages to Judah and warned of judgment for disobedience while also offering hope for restoration. 

In the New Testament, Jesus Christ, the Messiah, is born in Judea and is recognized as the King of the Jews (<ref="Mat.2.2">Mat.2.2</ref>). The early Christian church began in Jerusalem, and many of the first converts were Jews (Acts 2). 

Throughout the Bible, God's covenant relationship with the people of Judah, the Jews, and the inhabitants of Judea remains a central theme, highlighting His faithfulness, judgment, and redemptive purposes for all nations through the Jewish Messiah, Jesus Christ.

entries.name: Kenites
entries.brief: A nomadic tribe friendly to the Israelites
entries.short: The Kenites were a nomadic tribe who lived in the region of Canaan and were generally friendly to the Israelites, often providing them with assistance and support.
entries.article:
The Kenites were a nomadic tribe mentioned throughout the Old Testament. They lived in the region of Canaan and were generally friendly to the Israelites, often providing them with assistance and support. 

The Kenites are first mentioned in <ref="Gen.15.19">Gen.15.19</ref> as one of the tribes inhabiting the land that God promised to give to Abraham's descendants. In <ref="Num.24.21">Num.24.21</ref>, the Kenites are described as having a strong and secure dwelling place, possibly indicating their skill in metalworking and their strategic location. 

During the Israelites' conquest of Canaan, the Kenites, particularly Hobab (also known as Jethro), Moses' father-in-law, joined the tribe of Judah and settled in the Negev region (<ref="Jdg.1.16">Jdg.1.16</ref>). The Kenites maintained a close relationship with the Israelites, as evidenced by the story of Jael, a Kenite woman who killed Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army, aiding the Israelite victory (<ref="Jdg.4.11, 17-22; 5.24">Jdg.4.11, 17-22; 5.24</ref>). 

The Kenites' loyalty to the Israelites is further demonstrated when Saul, during his campaign against the Amalekites, warned the Kenites to separate themselves from the Amalekites to avoid being destroyed along with them (<ref="1Sa.15.6">1Sa.15.6</ref>). The Kenites heeded this warning and remained on friendly terms with the Israelites. 

Later, during David's time as a fugitive from Saul, he sent gifts to the Kenites, among other friendly tribes, acknowledging their support (<ref="1Sa.27.10; 30.29">1Sa.27.10; 30.29</ref>). 

In <ref="1Ch.2.55">1Ch.2.55</ref>, the Kenites are mentioned as scribes living in Jabez, suggesting that some Kenites may have taken on administrative roles within Israelite society. 

Throughout the biblical narrative, the Kenites are portrayed as a friendly and supportive tribe to the Israelites, playing a role in their early history and settlement in the Promised Land.

entries.name: Korah
entries.brief: Son of Hebron, descendant of Caleb
entries.short: Korah, son of Hebron, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Korah was a son of Hebron and a descendant of Caleb from the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.43">1Ch.2.43</ref>). He was born in the region of Judah during the period of the judges.

entries.name: Levi
entries.brief: Son of Jacob; progenitor of the Levites
entries.short: Levi, son of Jacob and Leah, was the progenitor of the Levites, the priestly tribe of Israel.
entries.article: Levi was the third son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and Leah (<ref="Gen.29.34">Gen.29.34</ref>). Along with his brother Simeon, he took revenge on the Shechemites for the rape of their sister Dinah (<ref="Gen.34.25-31">Gen.34.25-31</ref>). Jacob rebuked them for this act on his deathbed (<ref="Gen.49.5-7">Gen.49.5-7</ref>). Levi had three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari (<ref="Gen.46.11">Gen.46.11</ref>; <ref="Exo.6.16">Exo.6.16</ref>). His descendants, the Levites, were set apart as the priestly tribe (<ref="Exo.32.26-29">Exo.32.26-29</ref>; <ref="Num.3.5-13">Num.3.5-13</ref>). They were responsible for the tabernacle and its services (<ref="Num.1.47-54">Num.1.47-54</ref>; 3.14-39; 4.1-49; 8.5-26). The Levites were given cities throughout Israel, but no territorial inheritance (<ref="Num.35.1-8">Num.35.1-8</ref>; <ref="Jos.21.1-42">Jos.21.1-42</ref>). Notable Levites include Moses, Aaron, and Samuel. The Levites are frequently mentioned in the historical and prophetic books of the Old Testament, as well as in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. In the New Testament, Levites are mentioned in connection with the temple and its services (<ref="Luk.10.32">Luk.10.32</ref>; <ref="Jhn.1.19">Jhn.1.19</ref>; <ref="Act.4.36">Act.4.36</ref>). The Levitical priesthood is contrasted with the superior priesthood of Christ (<ref="Heb.7.1-28">Heb.7.1-28</ref>).

entries.name: Maacah
entries.brief: Caleb's concubine; mother of Sheber and Tirhanah
entries.short: Maacah, Caleb's concubine, was the mother of Sheber and Tirhanah.
entries.article: Maacah was a concubine of Caleb, the son of Hezron (<ref="1Ch.2.48">1Ch.2.48</ref>). She is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, specifically in the line of Caleb. Maacah gave birth to two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. No further information is provided about Maacah or her sons in the biblical record. Her inclusion in the genealogy highlights the complex family structures of the period and the importance of documenting lineage in ancient Israel.

entries.name: Maaz
entries.brief: Son of Ram, from the tribe of Judah
entries.short: Maaz was a son of Ram, a descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Maaz was a son of Ram, who was a descendant of Judah, as recorded in the genealogy found in 1Chronicles 2 (<ref="1Ch.2.27">1Ch.2.27</ref>). He is mentioned only in this genealogical list and no further information is provided about his life or role in the biblical narrative. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of Judah, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and highlights the descendants of Ram, who was a grandson of Judah. Maaz's inclusion in this list serves to establish the continuity of the tribe of Judah and its prominent figures. As with many individuals mentioned in biblical genealogies, the lack of additional details about Maaz suggests that the primary purpose of his mention is to maintain the historical record of the family line.

entries.name: Machbenah
entries.brief: Daughter or town founded by Sheva
entries.short: Machbenah was a descendant or town of Caleb, the son of Hezron, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Machbenah is mentioned as a daughter or a town of Sheva in the genealogy of Caleb, the son of Hezron, who was a descendant of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.49">1Ch.2.49</ref>). The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of Judah and highlights the descendants of Hezron, including Caleb. Machbenah is listed as one of the descendants of Caleb, along with several other individuals and clans. No further information is provided about Machbenah's life, occupation, or role in the biblical narrative. The mention of Machbenah in this genealogical record serves to establish the continuity of Caleb's lineage and the growth of his clan within the tribe of Judah. As with many individuals mentioned in biblical genealogies, the lack of additional details about Machbenah suggests that the primary purpose of the mention is to maintain the historical record of the family line.

entries.name: Machir
entries.brief: Son of Manasseh; father (ie re-founder) of Gilead
entries.short: Machir, the son of Manasseh, was the father  (ie re-founder) of Gilead and a prominent figure in the tribe of Manasseh.
entries.article: Machir was the son of Manasseh and the father  (ie re-founder) of Gilead, making him a significant ancestor of the tribe of Manasseh (<ref="Gen.50.23">Gen.50.23</ref>; <ref="Num.26.29">Num.26.29</ref>; <ref="1Ch.7.14">1Ch.7.14</ref>). He is mentioned numerous times throughout the Old Testament, often in relation to the settlement and inheritance of the tribe of Manasseh. Machir's descendants, known as the Machirites, formed a substantial portion of the tribe (<ref="Num.26.29">Num.26.29</ref>; <ref="Jos.17.1">Jos.17.1</ref>). They were known for their military prowess and were praised in the Song of Deborah (<ref="Jdg.5.14">Jdg.5.14</ref>). The Machirites, along with the Reubenites and Gadites, conquered and settled in the land of Gilead, east of the Jordan River (<ref="Num.32.39-40">Num.32.39-40</ref>; <ref="Deu.3.15">Deu.3.15</ref>; <ref="Jos.13.31">Jos.13.31</ref>). Machir's daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, appealed to Moses for the right to inherit their father's property in the absence of male heirs, setting a precedent for inheritance laws (<ref="Num.27.1">Num.27.1</ref>; 36.1; <ref="Jos.17.3">Jos.17.3</ref>). Machir's descendants continued to play a role in the tribe of Manasseh, with some even marrying into the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.21,23">1Ch.2.21,23</ref>).

entries.name: Madmannah
entries.brief: Descendant of Caleb, son of Hezron
entries.short: Madmannah was a descendant of Caleb, the son of Hezron, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Madmannah is mentioned in the genealogy of Caleb, the son of Hezron, who was a descendant of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.49">1Ch.2.49</ref>). The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of Judah and highlights the descendants of Hezron, including Caleb. Madmannah is listed as one of the descendants of Caleb, along with several other individuals and clans. No further information is provided about Madmannah's life, occupation, or role in the biblical narrative. The mention of Madmannah in this genealogical record serves to establish the continuity of Caleb's lineage and the growth of his clan within the tribe of Judah. As with many individuals mentioned in biblical genealogies, the lack of additional details about Madmannah suggests that the primary purpose of the mention is to maintain the historical record of the family line.

entries.name: Maon
entries.brief: Son of Shammai, a descendant of Caleb.
entries.short: Maon, a son of Shammai, was a descendant of Caleb.
entries.article: Maon was a descendant of Caleb, the son of Hezron, from the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Shammai and is mentioned in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants (<ref="1Ch.2.45">1Ch.2.45</ref>).

entries.name: Mareshah
entries.brief: Son of Mesha, re-founder of Hebron.
entries.short: Mareshah, a son of Mesha, was the father and re-founder of Hebron.
entries.article: Mareshah was a son of Mesha, son of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, from the tribe of Judah. He restored and re-founded Hebron which had been given to his father (Josh <ref="14.3">14.3</ref>) who removed the Anakim who inhabited it (<ref="Jdg.1.20">Jdg.1.20</ref>). Mareshah is mentioned in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants (<ref="1Ch.2.42">1Ch.2.42</ref>).

entries.name: Menuhoth
entries.brief: A clan descended from Caleb.
entries.short: Menuhoth, a clan descended from Caleb, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Menuhoth is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, specifically in the lineage of Caleb, the son of Hur (<ref="1Ch.2.52">1Ch.2.52</ref>). The text states that Caleb's sons included the clans of Ithrites, Puthites, Shumathites, and Mishraites, and that from these clans came the people of Zorah and Eshtaol. Menuhoth is listed among these clans, suggesting that they were a family group descended from Caleb.

entries.name: Mesha
entries.brief: Son of Caleb and founder of Ziph.
entries.short: Mesha, a son of Caleb, was the  father (ie founder) of Ziph.
entries.article: Mesha was a son of Caleb, the son of Hezron from the tribe of Judah. He founded (or fathered) Ziph.  (<ref="1Ch.2.42">1Ch.2.42</ref>).

entries.name: Mishraites
entries.brief: A clan descended from Shobal, of the tribe of Judah.
entries.short: The Mishraites were a clan descended from Shobal, who was a descendant of Judah through Caleb.
entries.article:
The Mishraites are mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.53">1Ch.2.53</ref> as one of the clans that descended from Shobal, a descendant of Judah through Caleb. This reference appears in the context of a genealogical record that traces the lineage of the tribe of Judah, providing insight into the various families and clans within the tribe. 

Apart from being listed as a clan descended from Shobal, no additional information is given about the Mishraites. The genealogy does not specify any notable individuals within the clan or provide details about their specific roles, occupations, or contributions to the tribe of Judah. 

The mention of the Mishraites in this genealogical context serves to highlight the complex family structures within the tribe of Judah and the importance of tracing lineage in ancient Israelite society. It also demonstrates the thoroughness of the chronicler in recording even the smaller clans and families within the larger tribal framework, preserving their names and place in history.

entries.name: Molid
entries.brief: Son of Abisur, of the tribe of Judah.
entries.short: Molid was the son of Abisur and Abihail, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article:
Molid is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.29">1Ch.2.29</ref> as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Abisur and his wife, Abihail. 

The genealogy in this passage traces the descendants of Judah, one of the twelve sons of Israel (or 'Jacob') (Israel), and provides insight into the family lines within the tribe. Molid is listed as a member of the clan of Jerahmeel, which was one of the major families within Judah. 

Apart from being named as the son of Abisur and Abihail, no additional information is provided about Molid's life, occupation, or role within the tribe. The genealogical record serves primarily to establish the lineage and family connections within Judah, rather than to provide detailed accounts of each individual. 

The inclusion of Molid in this genealogy highlights the importance of family heritage and tribal identity in ancient Israelite society. It also demonstrates the meticulous record-keeping of the chronicler in preserving the names and relationships of even the lesser-known members of the tribe. 

As with many of the individuals mentioned in these genealogies, Molid's contribution to the overall narrative of Israel's history may be limited, but his presence in the record helps to paint a more complete picture of the people and families that made up the nation.

entries.name: Moza
entries.brief: Son of Caleb by his concubine Ephah
entries.short: Moza was a son of Caleb, the renowned spy, by his concubine Ephah.
entries.article: Moza was one of the sons of Caleb, the son of Hezron, by his concubine Ephah (<ref="1Ch.2.46">1Ch.2.46</ref>). Caleb was one of the twelve spies sent by Moses to scout out Canaan (<ref="Num.13.6">Num.13.6</ref>). Along with Joshua, he gave a good report and was permitted to enter the promised land (<ref="Num.14.30">Num.14.30</ref>). No other details are given about Moza's life. He is not to be confused with the Benjamite Moza mentioned in the genealogies of Saul (<ref="1Ch.8.36-37, 9">1Ch.8.36-37, 9</ref>:42-43).

entries.name: Nadab
entries.brief: Son of Shammai, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.short: Nadab was a son of Shammai, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
entries.article:
Nadab is mentioned briefly in <ref="1Ch.2.28">1Ch.2.28</ref> and <ref="1Ch.2.30">1Ch.2.30</ref> as one of the sons of Shammai, a descendant of Judah through his son Jerahmeel. This reference appears in a genealogical record that traces the lineage of the tribe of Judah, providing insight into the family lines within the tribe. 

In the genealogy, Shammai is listed as the son of Onam, who was the son of Jerahmeel (<ref="1Ch.2.26-28">1Ch.2.26-28</ref>). Nadab is named alongside his brother Abishur as the sons of Shammai (<ref="1Ch.2.28">1Ch.2.28</ref>). 

Apart from being listed as a son of Shammai, no additional information is provided about Nadab's life, character, or role within the tribe of Judah. His mention in the genealogy serves primarily to establish his place within the family line and to contribute to the overall record of the tribe's history and lineage. 

The inclusion of Nadab in this genealogical record demonstrates the importance of family heritage and tribal identity in ancient Israelite society. These records helped establish the legitimacy of land claims, leadership roles, and the preservation of the tribe's history and connection to their ancestors.

entries.name: Nahshon
entries.brief: Son of Amminadab, leader of Judah, ancestor of David.
entries.short: Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, was a leader of the tribe of Judah during the Exodus and an ancestor of King David and Jesus Christ.
entries.article:
Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, was a prominent figure in the tribe of Judah during the Israelites' exodus from Egypt and their subsequent wilderness journey. He is mentioned in several books of the Bible, including Exodus, Numbers, Ruth, 1 Chronicles, Matthew, and Luke. 

According to <ref="Exo.6.23">Exo.6.23</ref>, Nahshon was the brother-in-law of Aaron, as his sister Elisheba was married to Aaron. This connection to the priestly family highlights Nahshon's significant status within the tribe of Judah. 

In <ref="Num.1.7">Num.1.7</ref> and <ref="Num.2.3">Num.2.3</ref>, Nahshon is identified as the leader of the tribe of Judah during the census and the arrangement of the Israelite camp in the wilderness. As the head of Judah, he was responsible for a large portion of the Israelite population and held a position of authority and responsibility. 

Nahshon's leadership role is further emphasized in <ref="Num.7.12,17">Num.7.12,17</ref>, where he is the first of the tribal leaders to present offerings at the dedication of the tabernacle. His offering, like those of the other leaders, included silver and gold vessels, as well as animals for sacrifice. 

In <ref="Num.10.14">Num.10.14</ref>, Nahshon is mentioned again as the leader of the tribe of Judah when the Israelites set out from Mount Sinai, following the order of march determined by God. 

The genealogies in <ref="Rut.4.20, 1">Rut.4.20, 1</ref> Chronicles <ref="Rut.2.10-11">Rut.2.10-11</ref>, <ref="Mat.1.4">Mat.1.4</ref>, and <ref="Luk.3.32">Luk.3.32</ref> identify Nahshon as an ancestor of King David and, consequently, of Jesus Christ. This lineage underscores the importance of Nahshon's role in the history of Israel and God's plan of redemption. 

Nahshon's life and leadership during the exodus and wilderness journey demonstrate his faithfulness and obedience to God. His prominent position within the tribe of Judah and his place in the lineage of David and Jesus make him a significant figure in the biblical narrative.

entries.name: Naphtali
entries.brief: Son of Jacob, founder of the tribe of Naphtali.
entries.short: Naphtali, the sixth son of Jacob and second son of Bilhah, was the founder of the Israelite tribe that bore his name.
entries.article:
Naphtali was the sixth son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and the second son of Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant (<ref="Gen.30.8; 35.25">Gen.30.8; 35.25</ref>). His birth was celebrated by Rachel, who had been struggling with infertility. She named him Naphtali, saying, "With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed" (<ref="Gen.30.8">Gen.30.8</ref>). 

As one of the twelve tribes of Israel, Naphtali played a significant role in the history of God's chosen people. During the Exodus, the tribe of Naphtali was led by Ahira son of Enan (<ref="Num.1.15">Num.1.15</ref>) and was counted among the Israelite tribes in the wilderness (<ref="Num.1.42-43; 26.48-50">Num.1.42-43; 26.48-50</ref>). 

In the arrangement of the Israelite camp, Naphtali was positioned on the north side, along with the tribes of Dan and Asher (<ref="Num.2.29">Num.2.29</ref>). The tribe also had representatives among the twelve spies sent to explore Canaan (<ref="Num.13.14">Num.13.14</ref>) and had a designated leader, Pedahel son of Ammihud, during the allocation of the Promised Land (<ref="Num.34.28">Num.34.28</ref>). 

The territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali was in the northern part of Canaan, bordering Asher, Zebulun, and Issachar (<ref="Jos.19.32-39">Jos.19.32-39</ref>). The region was known for its fertile lands and abundant resources, as reflected in Jacob's blessing: "Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns" (<ref="Gen.49.21">Gen.49.21</ref>) and Moses' blessing: "Naphtali is abounding with the favor of the Lord and is full of his blessing; he will inherit southward to the lake" (<ref="Deu.33.23">Deu.33.23</ref>). 

Throughout Israel's history, the tribe of Naphtali played various roles. They participated in the battles against Sisera (<ref="Jdg.4.6, 10; 5.18">Jdg.4.6, 10; 5.18</ref>) and the Midianites (<ref="Jdg.6.35; 7.23">Jdg.6.35; 7.23</ref>). The tribe also provided skilled warriors to support David (<ref="1Ch.12.34, 40">1Ch.12.34, 40</ref>) and was known for its wise and articulate people (<ref="Jdg.5.18">Jdg.5.18</ref>; Psalm <ref="Jdg.68.27">Jdg.68.27</ref>). 

In the New Testament, Naphtali is mentioned in connection with Jesus' ministry in the region of Galilee (<ref="Mat.4.13, 15">Mat.4.13, 15</ref>), fulfilling the prophecy of <ref="Isa.9.1">Isa.9.1</ref>. The tribe is also listed among the twelve tribes of Israel sealed by God in the book of Revelation (<ref="Rev.7.6">Rev.7.6</ref>).

entries.name: Nathan
entries.brief: Son of Attai, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.short: Nathan, the son of Attai, is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
entries.article:
Nathan is briefly mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.36">1Ch.2.36</ref> as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is identified as the son of Attai and the father of Zabad. 

The genealogical record in 1Chronicles 2 traces the descendants of Judah, one of the twelve sons of Israel (or 'Jacob') and the founder of the tribe that bears his name. This genealogy includes several prominent figures in Israelite history, such as Caleb, Boaz, and David. 

Nathan's mention in this genealogy serves to establish his place within the lineage of Judah and to demonstrate the continuity of the tribe through the generations. However, beyond his identification as the son of Attai and the father of Zabad, no further details are provided about Nathan's life, character, or role within the tribe. 

The inclusion of Nathan in this genealogical record highlights the importance of family lineage and tribal identity in ancient Israelite society. These genealogies served to establish the legitimacy of land claims, leadership roles, and the preservation of the tribe's history and connection to their ancestors.

entries.name: Nethanel
entries.brief: Brother of David
entries.short: Nethanel was a son of Jesse and brother of King David.
entries.article: Nethanel was the fourth son of Jesse and thus a brother of King David (<ref="1Ch.2.14">1Ch.2.14</ref>). He was born in Bethlehem. No other details are recorded about his life in the Bible. As a son of Jesse, he would have grown up as a shepherd alongside his brothers.

entries.name: Obed
entries.brief: Descendant of Judah
entries.short: Obed was a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel.
entries.article: Obed was a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel (<ref="1Ch.2.37-38">1Ch.2.37-38</ref>). He was the son of Ephlal and the father of Jehu. Obed is mentioned in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, which is part of the larger genealogy of the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Onam
entries.brief: Descendant of Judah, son of Jerahmeel
entries.short: Onam was a descendant of Judah, the son of Jerahmeel, and had two sons, Shammai and Jada.
entries.article: Onam was a descendant of Judah, the son of Jerahmeel (<ref="1Ch.2.26, 28">1Ch.2.26, 28</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, which lists the descendants of Judah's sons. Onam was the son of Jerahmeel and had two sons of his own, Shammai and Jada (<ref="1Ch.2.28">1Ch.2.28</ref>). The genealogy of Judah in 1Chronicles 2 provides insight into the family lines and clans within the tribe of Judah. Onam's mention in this genealogy suggests that he was a significant figure within the Jerahmeelite clan.

entries.name: Onan
entries.brief: Son of Judah
entries.short: Onan was the second son of Judah, who was punished by God for his wicked actions.
entries.article: Onan was the second son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shua (<ref="Gen.38.4">Gen.38.4</ref>; <ref="1Ch.2.3">1Ch.2.3</ref>). After the death of his older brother Er, Judah instructed Onan to marry Er's widow, Tamar, and produce an heir for his brother (<ref="Gen.38.8">Gen.38.8</ref>). However, Onan, knowing that the child would not be his own, practiced coitus interruptus to avoid providing an heir for his brother (<ref="Gen.38.9">Gen.38.9</ref>). This act was displeasing to the Lord, and as a result, God put Onan to death (<ref="Gen.38.10">Gen.38.10</ref>). Onan's death left Tamar without an heir and set the stage for the unusual events that followed, which ultimately led to the birth of Perez and Zerah, twin sons of Judah and Tamar (<ref="Gen.38.27-30">Gen.38.27-30</ref>). Onan is also mentioned in the genealogies of Judah (<ref="Gen.46.12">Gen.46.12</ref>; <ref="Num.26.19">Num.26.19</ref>; <ref="1Ch.2.3">1Ch.2.3</ref>).

entries.name: Oren
entries.brief: Son of Jerahmeel
entries.short: Oren was a son of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Oren was one of the sons of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.25">1Ch.2.25</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, which lists the descendants of Judah's sons and grandsons. Jerahmeel was the son of Hezron, who was the son of Perez, one of Judah's twin sons born to Tamar (<ref="1Ch.2.5, 9">1Ch.2.5, 9</ref>). The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 provides insight into the family lines and clans within the tribe of Judah. Oren's mention in this genealogy suggests that he was a significant figure within the Jerahmeelite clan. However, no further details about Oren's life or role are provided in the Bible.

entries.name: Ozem
entries.brief: Brother of David
entries.short: Ozem was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse.
entries.article: Ozem was one of the sons of Jesse and a brother of King David (<ref="1Ch.2.15">1Ch.2.15</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, which lists the descendants of Jesse. Ozem is named as the sixth son of Jesse, with his brothers being Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethanel, Raddai, and David (<ref="1Ch.2.13-15">1Ch.2.13-15</ref>). The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 provides insight into the family background of David, Israel's most famous king. However, no further details about Ozem's life or role are provided in the Bible.

entries.name: Pelet
entries.brief: Son of Jahdai, descendant of Judah
entries.short: Pelet, a son of Jahdai, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1Chronicles 2.
entries.article: Pelet was a son of Jahdai, according to the genealogy of Judah in <ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>. He is listed among the descendants of Caleb, the son of Hezron. No other information is provided about Pelet's life or role. His mention in the genealogy suggests that he was part of the tribe of Judah and lived during the period of Israel's settlement in Canaan or the early monarchy.

entries.name: Peleth
entries.brief: Son of Jonathan, descendant of Jerahmeel
entries.short: Peleth, a son of Jonathan and descendant of Jerahmeel, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Peleth was a son of Jonathan and a descendant of Jerahmeel, according to the genealogy of Judah in <ref="1Ch.2.33">1Ch.2.33</ref>. Jerahmeel was the firstborn son of Hezron, who was a grandson of Judah. Peleth is listed along with his brother Zaza as sons of Jonathan. No further details are provided about Peleth's life or role. His inclusion in the genealogy indicates he was part of the tribe of Judah and lived during the period of Israel's settlement in Canaan or the early monarchy.

entries.name: Perez
entries.brief: Son of Judah, ancestor of David and Jesus
entries.short: Perez, son of Judah and Tamar, was an ancestor of King David and Jesus Christ.
entries.article: Perez was the son of Judah and Tamar, born in unusual circumstances described in Genesis 38. He was the twin brother of Zerah and was named Perez (meaning "breach" or "breaking forth") because he broke out first during the delivery (<ref="Gen.38.29">Gen.38.29</ref>). Perez became the ancestor of a prominent clan within the tribe of Judah (<ref="Num.26.20-21">Num.26.20-21</ref>). He is mentioned in the genealogy of King David (<ref="Rut.4.12,18">Rut.4.12,18</ref>; <ref="1Ch.2.4-5">1Ch.2.4-5</ref>) and is an ancestor of several notable figures, including Hezron, Caleb, and Nahshon (<ref="1Ch.2.5,9,10">1Ch.2.5,9,10</ref>). The descendants of Perez were among those who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (<ref="Neh.11.4,6">Neh.11.4,6</ref>). Most significantly, Perez is listed in the genealogies of Jesus Christ in both <ref="Mat.1.3">Mat.1.3</ref> and <ref="Luk.3.33">Luk.3.33</ref>, highlighting his important role in the lineage of the Messiah.

entries.name: Puthites
entries.brief: A clan from the tribe of Judah
entries.short: The Puthites were a clan from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: The Puthites were a clan mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.53">1Ch.2.53</ref>). They are listed among the descendants of Salma, who was from the lineage of Caleb, one of the twelve spies sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan (<ref="Num.13.6">Num.13.6</ref>). The Puthites, along with the Shumathites and the Mishraites, were clans that originated from Kiriath-jearim, a city in Judah.

entries.name: Raddai
entries.brief: One of David's brothers, son of Jesse
entries.short: Raddai was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse.
entries.article: Raddai is mentioned in the genealogy of David as one of his brothers, a son of Jesse from Bethlehem (<ref="1Ch.2.14">1Ch.2.14</ref>). He is listed among David's seven brothers, including Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethaneel, Ozem, and the unnamed seventh brother. Raddai was likely born and raised in Bethlehem, where Jesse's family lived. However, no further information is provided about Raddai in the Bible, and he is not mentioned in the narrative of David's life or reign. His inclusion in the genealogy serves to establish David's family background and lineage.

entries.name: Raham
entries.brief: Son of Shema and founder of Jorkeam, of Judah
entries.short: Raham was the son of Shema and the father or founder of Jorkeam, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Raham is mentioned briefly in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.44">1Ch.2.44</ref>). He was the son of Shema and the father or founder of Jorkeam. No additional information is provided about Raham in the Bible. His mention in the genealogy serves to trace the lineage of certain families within the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Ram
entries.brief: Firstborn son of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah
entries.short: Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Ram is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah as the firstborn son of Jerahmeel (<ref="1Ch.2.25, 27">1Ch.2.25, 27</ref>). Jerahmeel was a descendant of Judah through his son Hezron. Ram had two brothers, Bunah and Oren, and a half-brother named Onam. The genealogy also mentions Ram's sons, Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. No further details are provided about Ram or his descendants in the Bible. The inclusion of Ram in the genealogy serves to document the family lines within the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Rechab
entries.brief: Ancestor of the Rechabites, who were faithful to God
entries.short: Rechab was the ancestor of the Rechabites, a nomadic tribe known for their faithfulness to God's commands.
entries.article: Rechab was the father of Jehonadab (<ref="2Ki.10.15">2Ki.10.15</ref>) and the ancestor of the Rechabites, a nomadic tribe known for their strict adherence to God's commands (Jeremiah 35). The Rechabites were descendants of the Kenites, who were associated with the Israelites since the time of Moses (<ref="Jdg.1.16">Jdg.1.16</ref>). Jehonadab, son of Rechab, supported Jehu in his purge of Baal worship in Israel (<ref="2Ki.10.15-23">2Ki.10.15-23</ref>). The Rechabites were known for their obedience to the commands of their ancestor Jonadab, which included abstaining from wine, not building houses, not sowing seed, and not planting vineyards (<ref="Jer.35.6-7">Jer.35.6-7</ref>). When the prophet Jeremiah tested their obedience by offering them wine, they refused, demonstrating their commitment to their ancestral vows (<ref="Jer.35.1-11">Jer.35.1-11</ref>). God commended the Rechabites for their faithfulness and promised that they would always have a descendant to serve Him (<ref="Jer.35.18-19">Jer.35.18-19</ref>). The example of the Rechabites stands as a model of obedience and devotion to God in the midst of a society that had largely abandoned His ways.

entries.name: Regem
entries.brief: Son of Jahdai, of the tribe of Judah
entries.short: Regem was a son of Jahdai, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Regem is mentioned briefly in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>). He was one of the sons of Jahdai, who was a descendant of Judah through Caleb, the son of Hezron. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of several prominent families within the tribe of Judah. No additional information is provided about Regem or his role within the tribe. His inclusion in the genealogy serves to document the family lines and descendants of Judah.

entries.name: Rekem
entries.brief: Son of Hebron, of the tribe of Judah
entries.short: Rekem was a son of Hebron, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Rekem is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.43, 44">1Ch.2.43, 44</ref>). He was one of the sons of Hebron, who was a descendant of Caleb, the son of Hezron. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of several prominent families within the tribe of Judah. Rekem is listed alongside his brothers Jorkeam, Shammai, and Shema (<ref="1Ch.2.44">1Ch.2.44</ref>). No additional information is provided about Rekem or his role within the tribe. His inclusion in the genealogy serves to document the family lines and descendants of Judah.

entries.name: Reuben
entries.brief: Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah
entries.short: Reuben was the firstborn son of Jacob and Leah, and his descendants formed one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
entries.article: Reuben was the firstborn son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and Leah (<ref="Gen.29.32">Gen.29.32</ref>). As the firstborn, he held a position of prominence and was entitled to a double portion of the inheritance (<ref="Gen.49.3">Gen.49.3</ref>; <ref="Deu.21.17">Deu.21.17</ref>). However, Reuben lost his birthright due to his sin of sleeping with his father's concubine, Bilhah (<ref="Gen.35.22; 49.3-4">Gen.35.22; 49.3-4</ref>; <ref="1Ch.5.1">1Ch.5.1</ref>). Despite this, Reuben showed concern for his younger brother Joseph and tried to save him from their brothers' plot to kill him (<ref="Gen.37.21-22, 29">Gen.37.21-22, 29</ref>). Later, he offered to bear the blame if harm came to Benjamin on their journey to Egypt (<ref="Gen.42.37">Gen.42.37</ref>). When Jacob blessed his sons, he described Reuben as "unstable as water" and declared that he would not excel because of his past actions (<ref="Gen.49.3-4">Gen.49.3-4</ref>). The tribe of Reuben, along with the tribes of Gad and half of Manasseh, settled in the land east of the Jordan River (Numbers 32; <ref="Jos.13.15-23">Jos.13.15-23</ref>). They assisted the other tribes in conquering Canaan before returning to their inheritance (Joshua 22). In the time of the judges, the tribe of Reuben was criticized for not assisting Deborah and Barak in the fight against Sisera (<ref="Jdg.5.15-16">Jdg.5.15-16</ref>). The tribe of Reuben is mentioned in the visions of Ezekiel and Revelation, symbolizing its place among the restored tribes of Israel (<ref="Ezk.48.6-7, 31">Ezk.48.6-7, 31</ref>; <ref="Rev.7.5">Rev.7.5</ref>).

entries.name: Salma
entries.brief: Son of Hur, founder of Bethlehem
entries.short: Salma was the son of Hur and the  father (ie founder) of Bethlehem, as mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Salma is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.51">1Ch.2.51</ref> and <ref="1Ch.2.54">1Ch.2.54</ref> as the son of Hur, who was a descendant of Judah, though the text is difficult to interpret. He is described as the father (ie founder) of Bethlehem, which suggests that he was an ancestor of the people who inhabited the town of Bethlehem in Judah. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 lists the descendants of Judah, including the line of Caleb, which played a significant role in the history of Israel. In verse 54, Salma is also associated with the Netophathites, a group of people who lived in the town of Netophah, near Bethlehem (<ref="Ezr.2.22">Ezr.2.22</ref>; <ref="Neh.7.26">Neh.7.26</ref>). This connection further emphasizes Salma's link to the region of Bethlehem and its surrounding areas. As the father of Bethlehem, Salma's mention in the genealogy highlights the importance of this town, which later became the birthplace of King David and Jesus Christ.

entries.name: Salmon
entries.brief: Son of Nahshon; husband of Rahab; ancestor of David
entries.short: Salmon (or Sala) was the son of Nahshon and husband of Rahab - an ancestor of King David and Jesus Christ.
entries.article: Salmon (or Sala) is mentioned in several genealogies in the Bible, including <ref="1Ch.2.11">1Ch.2.11</ref>, <ref="Rut.4.20-21">Rut.4.20-21</ref>, <ref="Mat.1.4-5">Mat.1.4-5</ref>, and <ref="Luk.3.32">Luk.3.32</ref>. He was the son of Nahshon, who was a leader of the tribe of Judah during the Israelites' wilderness wanderings (<ref="Num.1.7; 2.3; 7.12">Num.1.7; 2.3; 7.12</ref>). Salmon married Rahab, the Canaanite woman who helped the Israelite spies in Jericho (Joshua 2; <ref="Num.6.22-25">Num.6.22-25</ref>). This marriage is significant because it demonstrates God's grace and the inclusion of Gentiles in the lineage of the Messiah. Salmon and Rahab's son was Boaz, who married Ruth, the Moabite woman (<ref="Rut.4.13, 21">Rut.4.13, 21</ref>). Boaz and Ruth's son was Obed, the father of Jesse, who was the father of King David (<ref="Rut.4.17, 22">Rut.4.17, 22</ref>). Thus, Salmon is an important figure in the genealogy of David and, consequently, in the lineage of Jesus Christ (<ref="Mat.1.5-6, 16">Mat.1.5-6, 16</ref>). The variations in the spelling of his name (Salmon or Sala) in different passages may be due to linguistic differences or scribal traditions.

entries.name: Segub
entries.brief: Son of Hezron; father of Jair
entries.short: Segub, son of Hezron, was the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in Gilead.
entries.article: Segub, mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.21-22">1Ch.2.21-22</ref>, was the son of Hezron and the father of Jair. Hezron, at the age of sixty, married the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead. This marriage produced Segub. Segub's son, Jair, became a prominent figure who possessed twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. The passage highlights the genealogical connection between Hezron, Segub, and Jair, emphasizing Jair's significance as a possessor of many cities in Gilead. This information is part of the larger genealogical record of the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Seled
entries.brief: Son of Nadab, died without children
entries.short: Seled, a son of Nadab, died without having any children.
entries.article: Seled is mentioned twice in <ref="1Ch.2.30">1Ch.2.30</ref> as a son of Nadab, who was a descendant of Judah. The passage states that Seled died without having any children. This brief mention of Seled is part of a genealogical record of the tribe of Judah, focusing on the descendants of Hezron. The fact that Seled died childless is significant in the context of genealogies, as it marks the end of a particular line of descent.

entries.name: Shaaph
entries.brief: Son of Jahdai, a Calebite
entries.short: Shaaph, a son of Jahdai, was a descendant of Caleb.
entries.article: Shaaph, mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.47">1Ch.2.47</ref>, was a son of Jahdai and a descendant of Caleb, the son of Hezron. He is listed among the descendants of Judah, specifically within the Calebite clan. No further information about Shaaph's life or his role within the family is provided in the biblical text. His mention in the genealogy serves to highlight the lineage of Caleb and the importance of family records in ancient Israelite society.

entries.name: Shallum
entries.brief: Son of Sismai, descendant of Judah
entries.short: Shallum, the son of Sismai, was a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel.
entries.article: Shallum, mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.40-41">1Ch.2.40-41</ref>, was the son of Sismai and a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel. He is listed in the genealogical records of the tribe of Judah. Shallum's son was named Jekamiah, and Jekamiah's son was named Elishama. The genealogy in this passage traces the descendants of Jerahmeel, highlighting the importance of family lineage and the preservation of ancestral records.

entries.name: Shammai
entries.brief: Son of Onam; father of Nadab and Abishur
entries.short: Shammai, the son of Onam, was the father of Nadab and Abishur, who were descendants of Jerahmeel, the son of Hezron.
entries.article: Shammai, mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.28,32">1Ch.2.28,32</ref>, was a descendant of Judah through the line of Hezron. He was the son of Onam and the grandson of Jerahmeel. Shammai had two sons, Nadab and Abishur, who are listed in the genealogical record of Judah. The text does not provide any specific details about Shammai's life or his role within the family. However, his inclusion in the genealogy highlights the importance of documenting and preserving family lineages, especially within the tribe of Judah, from which the Messiah would come. The mention of Shammai and his sons serves to trace the descendants of Judah and show the continuation of the family line through multiple generations.

entries.name: Sheber
entries.brief: Son of Caleb and his concubine Maacah
entries.short: Sheber was one of the sons born to Caleb and his concubine Maacah, as mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Sheber, mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.48">1Ch.2.48</ref>, was one of the sons of Caleb, a prominent figure in the tribe of Judah, born to his concubine Maacah. Sheber is listed among Caleb's descendants in the genealogy of Judah, which traces the lineage of the tribe from its early ancestors. The text does not provide any further details about Sheber's life, his role within the tribe, or any specific achievements. His mention in the genealogy serves to highlight the importance of family lineage and the recording of descendants in the biblical narrative. The inclusion of Sheber, along with his brothers, in the list of Caleb's sons born to his concubine Maacah, also sheds light on the social and familial practices of the time, where it was not uncommon for men to have multiple wives and concubines.

entries.name: Shelah
entries.brief: Judah's youngest son and his descendants
entries.short: Shelah, Judah's third son, and his descendants, the Shelanites.
entries.article:
Shelah was the third and youngest son of Judah, born to him in Chezib (<ref="Gen.38.5">Gen.38.5</ref>). After the deaths of his older brothers, Er and Onan, Judah promised Tamar, Er's widow, that Shelah would marry her when he grew up. However, Judah did not keep this promise (<ref="Gen.38.11,14,26">Gen.38.11,14,26</ref>). 

Shelah's descendants were called Shelanites (<ref="Num.26.20">Num.26.20</ref>) and were one of the clans of Judah. They were included in the census of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (<ref="Num.26.20">Num.26.20</ref>) and in the genealogies of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.3; 4.21">1Ch.2.3; 4.21</ref>). Shelah's descendants included potters and linen workers who lived in Judah (<ref="1Ch.4.21-23">1Ch.4.21-23</ref>).

entries.name: Shema
entries.brief: Son of Hebron, a Judahite
entries.short: Shema, a son of Hebron and descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Shema is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.43-44">1Ch.2.43-44</ref> as one of the sons of Hebron, who was a descendant of Judah. He is listed along with his brothers Korah, Tappuah, and Rekem. Shema's son was named Raham, and Raham's son was Jorkeam.

entries.name: Sheshan
entries.brief: Jerahmeelite whose daughter married his Egyptian servant
entries.short: Sheshan, a Jerahmeelite who gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant, Jarha.
entries.article: Sheshan was a member of the Jerahmeelite clan, which was part of the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned in the genealogical record of 1Chronicles 2. Sheshan had no sons, only daughters (v. 34). Faced with the prospect of his lineage ending, Sheshan took an unconventional step. He gave one of his daughters in marriage to his Egyptian servant, Jarha (v. 35). This act allowed Sheshan's line to continue through his daughter and his servant. The passage goes on to list the descendants of Sheshan through this union, indicating that his decision had a lasting impact on his family line. This account highlights the importance of preserving one's lineage and the measures taken to ensure its continuation, even if it meant crossing social boundaries.

entries.name: Sheva
entries.brief: Son of Caleb's concubine Maacah
entries.short: Sheva, a son of Caleb's concubine Maacah, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Sheva is briefly mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.49">1Ch.2.49</ref> as a son of Caleb's concubine Maacah. He appears in the genealogical record of the tribe of Judah, specifically within the family line of Caleb.

entries.name: Shobab
entries.brief: Son of Caleb and Azubah.
entries.short: Shobab was a son of Caleb and his wife Azubah.
entries.article: Shobab is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.18">1Ch.2.18</ref> as a son of Caleb, the son of Hezron, and his wife Azubah. This passage is part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, focusing on the descendants of Caleb. Shobab is listed along with his brothers Jesher and Ardon.

entries.name: Shobal
entries.brief: Son of Hur, founder of Kiriath-jearim, Judahite descendant.
entries.short: Shobal was a Judahite, the son of Hur and the father (ie founder) of Kiriath-jearim.
entries.article: Shobal is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.50,52">1Ch.2.50,52</ref> and <ref="1Ch.4.1,2">1Ch.4.1,2</ref> as a descendant of Judah through Hur, the son of Caleb, though the text is difficult to interpret. He is described as the father (ie founder) of Kiriath-jearim, a city in Judah. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 lists Shobal among the descendants of Hur, along with his brothers Salma and Hareph. In 1Chronicles 4, Shobal is mentioned again as the father of Reaiah, who was the father of Jahath. This passage also states that the families of Kiriath-jearim, including the Ithrites, Puthites, Shumathites, and Mishraites, were descended from Shobal. These clans were known for their various occupations, such as scribes, linen workers, and potters. Shobal's mention in the genealogies of Judah highlights his role as an ancestor of prominent families and clans within the tribe.

entries.name: Shua
entries.brief: Father of Canaanite wife of Judah, mother of Er, Onan, and Shelah.
entries.short: Shua was the father of a Canaanite woman, the wife of Judah, and the mother of Er, Onan, and Shelah.
entries.article: Shua is mentioned in <ref="Gen.38.2,12">Gen.38.2,12</ref> and <ref="1Ch.2.3">1Ch.2.3</ref> as the father of a Canaanite wife of Judah, one of the twelve sons of Israel (or 'Jacob'). Judah married Bath-shua, the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, and she bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. The narrative in Genesis 38 focuses on the story of Judah and Tamar, with Bath-shua's sons playing a significant role. Er, Judah's firstborn, was killed by God due to his wickedness, and Onan, who was obligated to provide an heir for his deceased brother, also displeased God and died. Bath-shua is not mentioned beyond her role as the mother of Judah's sons, and her Canaanite origin is significant in the context of the Israelites' relationship with the Canaanites in the Promised Land.

entries.name: Shumathites
entries.brief: A family of Kirjath-jearim, descendants of Judah.
entries.short: The Shumathites were a family from Kirjath-jearim, descendants of Judah through Shobal.
entries.article: The Shumathites are mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.53">1Ch.2.53</ref> as one of the families from Kirjath-jearim, along with the Ithrites, Puthites, and Mishraites. These families are listed as descendants of Shobal, who was a son of Hur and a grandson of Judah (<ref="1Ch.2.50">1Ch.2.50</ref>). Kirjath-jearim was a city in Judah, known for being the place where the Ark of the Covenant was kept for a period before being brought to Jerusalem by King David (<ref="1Sa.7.1-2">1Sa.7.1-2</ref>; <ref="1Ch.13.5-6">1Ch.13.5-6</ref>).

entries.name: Simeon
entries.brief: Son of Jacob and Leah, one of the twelve tribes.
entries.short: Simeon, the second son of Jacob and Leah, was the founder of the tribe of Simeon and played a role in the story of Joseph.
entries.article:
Simeon was the second son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and Leah, born after Reuben (<ref="Gen.29.33">Gen.29.33</ref>). He was one of the twelve sons of Jacob who became the founders of the twelve tribes of Israel. Simeon, along with his brother Levi, took violent revenge against the Shechemites for the rape of their sister Dinah (<ref="Gen.34.25-30">Gen.34.25-30</ref>). This action was condemned by their father, Jacob (<ref="Gen.49.5-7">Gen.49.5-7</ref>). 

When Joseph's brothers went to Egypt during the famine, Joseph took Simeon as a hostage until they brought their youngest brother, Benjamin (<ref="Gen.42.24,36; 43.23">Gen.42.24,36; 43.23</ref>). Simeon was later released and returned to Canaan with his brothers (<ref="Gen.46.10">Gen.46.10</ref>). 

The tribe of Simeon, descended from Simeon, was one of the twelve tribes of Israel. During the wilderness wanderings, the tribe of Simeon was led by Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai (<ref="Num.1.6; 2.12; 7.36; 10.19">Num.1.6; 2.12; 7.36; 10.19</ref>). The tribe's territory was located within the boundaries of Judah in the Negev (<ref="Jos.19.1,9">Jos.19.1,9</ref>; <ref="Jdg.1.3,17">Jdg.1.3,17</ref>). 

In later history, some from the tribe of Simeon migrated to Edom during the reign of Hezekiah (<ref="1Ch.4.42-43">1Ch.4.42-43</ref>). The tribe is mentioned in the visions of Ezekiel (<ref="Ezk.48.24,25,33">Ezk.48.24,25,33</ref>) and in the list of the sealed from the twelve tribes in Revelation (<ref="Rev.7.7">Rev.7.7</ref>).

entries.name: Sismai
entries.brief: Descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel.
entries.short: Sismai was a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Sismai is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.40">1Ch.2.40</ref> as a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel. He was the son of Eleasah and the father of Shallum. The genealogy in this passage traces the lineage of Jerahmeel, who was one of the sons of Hezron, a grandson of Judah. This genealogical record demonstrates the continued presence and development of the tribe of Judah, even through lesser-known branches of the family tree.

entries.name: Tamar
entries.brief: Judah's daughter-in-law who bore Perez and Zerah
entries.short: Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law who, after being wronged by him, bore twin sons Perez and Zerah.
entries.article: Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah, married first to his son Er and then to Onan (<ref="Gen.38.6-11">Gen.38.6-11</ref>). After being wronged by Judah, Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute and conceived twins by him (<ref="Gen.38.13-24">Gen.38.13-24</ref>). She gave birth to Perez and Zerah, who became ancestors of the tribe of Judah (<ref="Gen.38.29-30">Gen.38.29-30</ref>; <ref="Rut.4.12">Rut.4.12</ref>; <ref="1Ch.2.4">1Ch.2.4</ref>). Tamar is praised for her righteousness in contrast to Judah (<ref="Gen.38.26">Gen.38.26</ref>). She is mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus (<ref="Mat.1.3">Mat.1.3</ref>).

entries.name: Tappuah
entries.brief: Son of Hebron from the tribe of Judah
entries.short: Tappuah was a son of Hebron, a descendant of Judah.
entries.article: Tappuah is mentioned in <ref="1Ch.2.43">1Ch.2.43</ref> as one of the sons of Hebron. Hebron was a descendant of Judah through Caleb, making Tappuah a member of the tribe of Judah.

entries.name: Tirhanah
entries.brief: Son of Caleb by his concubine Maacah
entries.short: Tirhanah was a son of Caleb by his concubine Maacah, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.article: Tirhanah is mentioned briefly in <ref="1Ch.2.48">1Ch.2.48</ref> as one of the sons of Caleb by his concubine Maacah. He is listed along with his brothers Sheber and Shaaph. Caleb was a prominent figure from the tribe of Judah, one of the twelve spies sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan (<ref="Num.13.6">Num.13.6</ref>). The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the descendants of Judah, including Caleb's family.

entries.name: Uri
entries.brief: Father of Bezalel, the skilled craftsman
entries.short: Uri was the father of Bezalel, the skilled craftsman chosen by God to construct the tabernacle and its furnishings.
entries.article: Uri, the son of Hur from the tribe of Judah, is mentioned in <ref="Exo.31.2, 35">Exo.31.2, 35</ref>:30, and <ref="Exo.38.22">Exo.38.22</ref>, as well as <ref="1Ch.2.20">1Ch.2.20</ref>, as the father of Bezalel. Bezalel was the skilled craftsman chosen by God and filled with the Spirit of God to construct the tabernacle and its furnishings, including the ark of the covenant. Uri's grandson, Bezalel, is also mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in <ref="1Ch.2.20">1Ch.2.20</ref>, emphasizing the family's important role in the construction of the tabernacle. Apart from being the father of Bezalel, no other details are provided about Uri's life or his own role in the community.

entries.name: Zabad
entries.brief: Descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel
entries.short: Zabad was a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel.
entries.article: Zabad is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, specifically in the line of Jerahmeel. He was the son of Nathan and the father of Ephlal. Zabad is listed as part of the descendants of Sheshan, who had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha. This genealogy shows the intermarriage between Israelites and non-Israelites.

entries.name: Zaza
entries.brief: Son of Jonathan, descendant of Jerahmeel
entries.short: Zaza was a son of Jonathan and a descendant of Jerahmeel from the tribe of Judah.
entries.article: Zaza is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, specifically as a son of Jonathan and a descendant of Jerahmeel. Jerahmeel was one of the sons of Hezron, who was a grandson of Judah. The genealogy in 1Chronicles 2 traces the lineage of Judah's descendants, including the family line of Jerahmeel. Zaza is listed along with his brother Peleth as the sons of Jonathan.

entries.name: Zebulun
entries.brief: Israelite tribe, son of Jacob and Leah
entries.short: Zebulun was the tenth son of Jacob, the sixth and last of Leah, and his descendants formed one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
entries.article:
Zebulun was the tenth son of Israel (or 'Jacob') and the sixth and last son of Leah. He was born in Paddan-aram, and his name is derived from the Hebrew word meaning "honor" or "dwelling." The tribe of Zebulun played a significant role in Israel's history, being one of the twelve tribes that settled in the Promised Land. During the wilderness wanderings, the tribe of Zebulun was led by Eliab, son of Helon, and was positioned with the tribes of Judah and Issachar on the east side of the tabernacle. In the census taken in the wilderness, the tribe of Zebulun numbered 57,400 men of fighting age. 

The territory allotted to Zebulun was in the northern part of Canaan, bordered by Asher, Naphtali, and Issachar. It included the fertile plain of Jezreel and the coastal region along the Mediterranean Sea. The tribe of Zebulun was commended for their bravery and willingness to fight, as evidenced by their participation in the battles against Sisera and the Midianites. They were also known for their maritime skills and engaged in trade and commerce. 

Notable members of the tribe of Zebulun include Elon, who judged Israel for ten years, and Ibzan of Bethlehem, who was buried in the territory of Zebulun. The prophet Jonah also hailed from Gath-hepher, a town within Zebulun's borders. 

In the future distribution of the land described by Ezekiel, Zebulun is allocated a portion in the far north of Israel, with its boundaries stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Jordan River. The tribe of Zebulun is also mentioned in the book of Revelation as one of the twelve tribes sealed by God.

entries.name: Zerah
entries.brief: Son of Judah, twin of Perez
entries.short: Zerah, son of Judah and Tamar, was the twin brother of Perez and ancestor of Achan.
entries.article:
Zerah was the son of Judah and Tamar, and the twin brother of Perez. His birth is recorded in Genesis 38, where it is noted that he put out his hand first during delivery, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on his wrist. However, his brother Perez was actually born first, breaking out before him. 

Zerah's descendants are mentioned in various genealogies throughout the Old Testament. Most notably, Achan, the man who sinned by taking the devoted things during the conquest of Jericho, was from the tribe of Judah and the family of Zerah. The descendants of Zerah are also mentioned among those who lived in Jerusalem after the exile. In 1Chronicles 27, it is recorded that Shamhuth, from the clan of Zerah, was in charge of the fifth division of David's army. 

His descendants the Izrahites or Ezrahites included very wise men (<ref="1Ki.4.31">1Ki.4.31</ref>).  Ethan is also credited with composing Psalm 89 (Psalm <ref="1Ki.89.1">1Ki.89.1</ref>). Another notable Ezrahite was Heman, who was a singer and musician in the time of David and is mentioned as the author of Psalm 88 (Psalm <ref="1Ki.88.1">1Ki.88.1</ref>; <ref="1Ch.6.33">1Ch.6.33</ref>).  

Zerah is also included in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1, highlighting his significance in the lineage of the Messiah.

entries.name: Zeruiah
entries.brief: Sister of David; mother of Joab, Abishai, and Asahel
entries.short: Zeruiah, David's sister, was the mother of Joab, Abishai, and Asahel, who were among David's mighty men and military leaders.
entries.article: Zeruiah was the sister of King David and the mother of three of his most prominent military leaders: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Her sons played significant roles throughout David's reign, both in military campaigns and in political matters. Joab served as the commander of David's army, while Abishai and Asahel were also known for their bravery and skill in battle. Zeruiah's sons were fiercely loyal to David, though their actions sometimes brought them into conflict with the king. For example, Joab murdered Abner and Amasa, two of David's rivals, without the king's consent. Despite these tensions, David recognized the importance of Zeruiah's sons in establishing and maintaining his kingdom. The fact that Zeruiah is consistently mentioned as their mother highlights her significance in the family and her influence on her sons' roles in David's court.

entries.name: Zorathites
entries.brief: Judahite clan descended from Shobal
entries.short: The Zorathites were a Judahite clan descended from Shobal.
